title: Widespread Microbial Suppression and Functional Shifts in Wastewater Treatment Microbiomes Under Climate Warming
content:
Climate warming may fundamentally reshape engineered microbiomes. Global‐scale modelling reveals widespread microbial suppression, weakened community interactions and altered ecosystem functions in wastewater treatment plants, providing early warning of climate‐driven ecological vulnerabilities.

ABSTRACT
Climate warming is expected to reshape microbial communities, yet its impacts on engineered microbial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a deep‐learning framework to assess microbial responses to climate warming across global wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs). Under a +1.5°C warming perturbation, ~77% of analyzed microbial taxa showed predicted declines in relative abundance, accompanied by decreased weights in ~54% of reconstructed microbial associations. Keystone taxa were also predominantly predicted to decline, suggesting potential changes in community association structure under warming. From an exploratory ecological perspective, warming‐associated increases in viral abundance may further contribute to microbial suppression through enhanced viral pressure on key taxa. Taxonomically inferred functional profiles suggested warming was also associated with broad shifts in ecological functional profiles, including potential impairments in nutrient cycling. Notably, increases in methanogenesis‐associated taxa coupled with reduced methane oxidation suggested a potential imbalance in methane cycling. Together, these findings indicate that climate warming may substantially reshape the composition, interactions and ecological functioning of WWTP microbiomes. Our study provides a global assessment of climate‐associated risks in engineered microbial ecosystems and offers a basis for developing climate‐resilient wastewater management strategies.

title: Long‐Term Acclimation and Membrane Lipid Remodelling Enable Anaerobic Oxidation of Methane at Low‐pH by ‘Ca. Methanoperedens vercellensis’
content:
Anaerobic methanotrophic archaea from the genus ‘Ca. Methanoperedens’ are slow‐growing microorganisms utilizing a range of electron acceptors such as nitrate. A granular enrichment culture of ‘Ca. Methanoperedens vercellensis’ remains metabolically active during stepwise acidification of the medium down to pH 5.65, whereas its activity is inhibited by immediate acid stress. Long‐term acclimation potential of the biomass is enabled by remodelling of membrane lipid composition, a viable strategy for survival in acidic ecosystems.

ABSTRACT
Anaerobic methanotrophic archaea are key members of the methane cycle, preventing emissions of the potent greenhouse gas into the atmosphere. Previous studies of freshwater anaerobic methanotrophs targeted their activity at circumneutral pH whereas molecular ecology studies detected anaerobic methane oxidizers in acidic environments such as peatlands. However, it remains unclear whether they can adapt to low pH and sustain an effective biological methane filter under acidic conditions. Here, we show that a granular enrichment culture of the freshwater methanotroph ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’ remains metabolically active down to pH 5.65 with appropriate acclimation time while it loses activity when experiencing immediate acid stress. Population‐wide acclimation is required to support anaerobic methane oxidation at lower pH. Archaeal lipid analyses revealed an increased abundance of zwitterionic intact polar lipids over anionic lipids. This coincided with structural changes in biomass granules while methane oxidation rate and enrichment proportion of ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’ remained stable. These results demonstrate that ‘Ca. M. vercellensis’ remains metabolically active at lower pH values, despite increased maintenance energy requirements and the need for cytoplasmic pH homeostasis. Furthermore, they highlight that stress adaptations in slow‐growing microorganisms requires long‐term observation. Our findings provide new insights into methane cycling in acidic ecosystems.

title: Dynamics of inorganic nitrogen cycling, redox conditions, and microbial community composition in a floodplain soil induced by a heavy rainfall after summer drought
content:
Dynamics of inorganic nitrogen cycling, redox conditions, and microbial community composition in a floodplain soil induced by a heavy rainfall after summer drought
Johanna Schlögl, Clemens Karwautz, Lena Cramaro, Wolfgang Wanek, Judith Prommer, Theresa Böckle, Andreas Kappler, Stefan B. Haderlein, and Christian Griebler
Biogeosciences, 23, 8017–8037, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8017-2026, 2026
Climate change enhances the occurrence of summer droughts and heavy rainfall events in Central Europe. We investigated the response of inorganic nitrogen cycling, redox conditions and microbial community composition to an artificial heavy rain event following a drought in shallow arable soil. Redox conditions changed fast with the hydraulic event triggering nitrogen transport and turnover. Microbial communities remained rather stable in terms of composition but exhibited enzyme activity changes.

title: Valley-bottom wetland agricultural conversion and recovery shape greenhouse gas dynamics and soil organic carbon stocks in an African tropical highland system
content:
Valley-bottom wetland agricultural conversion and recovery shape greenhouse gas dynamics and soil organic carbon stocks in an African tropical highland system
Sharon Gubamwoyo, Sonja M. Leitner, Gabriele Weigelhofer, Damaris G. Kisha, Oswald Omuron, Dominik Henrik Zak, Thomas Hein, and Gretchen M. Gettel
Biogeosciences, 23, 8039–8061, https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-8039-2026, 2026
Wetlands regulate greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics, but data from tropical and sub-Saharan African wetlands are limited. This study measured N₂O, CO₂, and CH₄ fluxes in intact, recovering, and converted highland valley-bottom wetlands in Taita Hills, Kenya, to assess effects of conversion on GHG dynamics, biogeochemical drivers, and soil organic carbon stocks. Conversion shifted systems from CH₄- to N₂O-dominated, while intact wetlands had the highest SOC stocks.

title: Dominant Role of Soil Moisture in Controlling Nighttime Net Ecosystem Exchange in Sub‐Humid West African Ecosystems
content:
Abstract
Understanding the environmental controls on nighttime Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEEnight) in tropical ecosystems is essential for constraining carbon cycle processes under increasing climate variability. In this study, we analyzed 21 site‐years of eddy covariance and ancillary measurements from two contrasting ecosystems, a cultivated savannah and a dry forest in the sub‐humid zone of West Africa. Using mutual information (MI) and wavelet analysis, we examined how soil moisture and soil temperature, measured at two depths, influence NEEnight across seasons and contrasting rainfall regimes (normal, surplus, and deficient years). MI results consistently identified soil moisture as the dominant control on NEEnight across both ecosystems and seasons. Wavelet analysis revealed strong and persistent coherence between NEEnight and soil moisture over periods ranging from 16 to 128 nights, especially during dry and moistening seasons characterized by irregular rainfall. In contrast, soil temperature showed weaker and more intermittent coherence, mainly at shorter periods of 2–8 nights. In years with normal rainfall, lead‐lag relationships indicated that soil moisture tended to precede NEEnight by about four nights at the cultivated savannah, whereas the dry forest exhibited more complex and less temporally persistent relationships, particularly during deficient rainfall years. These findings highlight soil moisture's dominant role in regulating nighttime CO2 fluxes across these ecosystems. They further emphasize the need to incorporate moisture‐driven and scale‐dependent processes into carbon cycle models to better represent ecosystem respiration under increasing climate variability.

title: Regulation of Bacterial Community Diversity in Estuaries and Nearshore Waters on the Degradation of Terrestrial Dissolved Organic Matter
content:
Abstract
The global flux of terrestrial organic matter increases annually, while the fate of terrigenous dissolved organic matter (tDOM) in marine environments is not well understood. Little is known about how changing bacterial communities modulate the fate of tDOM at the molecular level. To explore how changing bacterial communities regulate the transformation of tDOM, microcosm incubations were conducted by inoculating indigenous, exogenous, and their mixed communities into the tDOM pool collected from low‐salinity surface water. Our results show that the enhanced diversity of bacterial communities, which promotes bacteria‐DOM interactions, along with the enrichment of the rare biosphere, facilitates the transformation of highly aromatic and unsaturated DOM. Shifts in bacterial communities with no diversity change do not necessarily promote the processing of tDOM. These findings imply that the mixing of freshwater and seawater enhances bacterial community diversity, facilitating the transformation of refractory tDOM, which provides new insights into the biogeochemical processes modulating the fate of tDOM in estuarine and coastal waters.

title: Decadal Changes in Three‐Dimensional Accumulation Features in the Western North Pacific
content:
Abstract
Using a three‐dimensional Markov chain framework, we investigate accumulation features in the western North Pacific (WNP) during 2003–2022. These accumulation features reflect the integrated effects of circulation and provide a physically meaningful indicator of how circulation variability reorganizes three‐dimensional transport in this complex system. Particles preferentially converge into three major accumulation cores: a northern core associated with the Kuroshio recirculation (KR), a southern open‐ocean core near the Mindanao Dome (MD), and a marginal‐sea core in the southern South China Sea (sSCS). Source‐sink relationships derived from the transition matrix reveal distinct supply pathways for each core. The KR, MD, and sSCS cores are primarily supplied by downstream Kuroshio recirculation, the locally recirculating flow bounded by the North Equatorial Current and North Equatorial Countercurrent, and Luzon Strait inflow followed by trapping within the regional cyclonic gyre, respectively. Water‐distance analysis in potential density‐potential spiciness space supports the Markov‐based source patterns. Inter‐layer exchange contributes about 15%–35% of net accumulation within the cores. Upward exchange is prominent toward the MD and sSCS cores, consistent with upwelling in the Mindanao Dome and South China Sea, whereas downward exchange is prominent toward the KR core, consistent with mode‐water subduction. Over the past two decades, accumulation has intensified in the KR and sSCS but weakened in the MD, driven by changes in current intensity and convergence ability in the WNP. These results suggest that recent circulation changes have enhanced retention in recirculation and marginal‐sea systems, while reducing long‐term mass convergence in open‐ocean regions.

title: The Response of the Upwelling Source Depth to Wind Stress Variability in the California Coastal Upwelling System
content:
Abstract
Coastal upwelling is responsible for sustaining some of the oceans' most productive ecosystems. In order to quantify and predict the resulting surface properties, such as sea surface temperature and nutrient content, it is useful to consider the depth (or range of depths) from which the upwelled water originates. Here, we investigate the effects of wind stress variability on the upwelling source depth in the California upwelling system using regional ocean simulations. We test the response of the mean source depth and its full distribution to three wind stress fields with the same temporal mean but different time dependencies of the variability (constant, monthly, and 6‐hourly). The results of our numerical experiments show that upwelling source depth is deeper when the wind stress varies on shorter timescales. We further show that this result is a direct consequence of the nonlinear response of the upwelling source depth to the variable wind stress on short timescales. Additionally, we find that the scaling relations previously predicted for the source depth as a function of a time‐independent wind stress do not seem to hold when the wind stress is time variable. This work highlights the importance of considering both the time‐mean and variability of the wind stress for understanding and predicting the upwelling source depth and corresponding properties of the upper ocean in coastal upwelling zones.

title: Comparative Phylogeography and Genetic Diversity Between Mainland and Island Populations of Common Ground Doves (Columbina passerina) and Their Parasitic Lice
content:
ABSTRACT
Island archipelagos are ideal natural laboratories for studying genetic variation in populations of organisms. However, relatively little attention has been given to parasites associated with hosts from oceanic islands. Here, we focus on Common Ground Doves (Columbina passerina) and two ecomorphs of parasitic lice, Physconelloides eurysema body lice and Columbicola passerinae wing lice. Both louse species parasitize C. passerina doves and their close relatives but differ in their dispersal abilities. The doves and lice are widespread across the Caribbean archipelago and adjacent continents. We were interested in two primary questions: (1) do doves and lice have congruent phylogeographic histories? and (2) do island populations of doves and lice have reduced genetic diversity compared to mainland populations? To address these questions, we used genomic data from doves and lice to reconstruct phylogenetic relationships, assess population genetic structure, and estimate measures of genetic diversity. We found that genetic structure was not consistently congruent among the doves and lice, suggesting movement of the doves that is not apparent from their genetic information. Doves and lice also have different phylogeographic histories. Doves likely originated in the Caribbean islands, whereas lice originated in the mainland or dispersed multiple times between the mainland and islands. We also did not find strong evidence that island populations of doves or lice have less genetic diversity compared to mainland populations. Our results highlight that hosts are the most immediate ‘island’ for their parasites, but varying dispersal abilities and island geography can lead to discordant phylogeographic patterns over time.

title: Evidence of Putative Mitonuclear Incompatibilities in the Bullock's and Baltimore Oriole Hybrid Zone
content:
ABSTRACT
Mitonuclear incompatibilities are genetic mismatches between mitochondrial and nuclear genomes that initially arise through hybridization. Although these incompatibilities can reduce hybrid fitness and contribute to reproductive isolation, they remain poorly understood in most avian hybrid zones. To investigate mitonuclear discordance in the extensively studied hybrid zone between Bullock's (Icterus bullockii) and Baltimore Orioles (I. galbula), we used whole‐genome resequencing and mitochondrial haplotyping to assign mitochondrial ancestry to 136 individuals previously characterized for their levels of nuclear genomic admixture. We detected a narrow mitochondrial cline across the hybrid zone and strong asymmetry in mitochondrial inheritance, with 83% of putative F1 hybrids having I. galbula mitochondrial ancestry, a pattern consistent with predictions from Darwin's corollary to Haldane's rule involving uniparentally inherited loci. Genome‐wide association analyses revealed nonrandom associations between mitochondrial haplotype and autosomal nuclear loci, notably including candidate genes with mitochondrial functions. Population‐specific signals of positive selection at these loci further suggest differential selective pressures linked to mitochondrial ancestry. Together, our results provide evidence that mitonuclear interactions may contribute to asymmetric introgression and the maintenance of species boundaries in this classic avian hybrid zone.

Acquisitive plant traits are favored during and following drought: Insights from two long‐term grassland experiments
content:
Abstract
Plant traits influence species responses to environmental change. Extreme drought alters plant traits at both individual and community levels, yet few studies have tracked whether these changes persist after drought or examined their relationships with ecosystem net primary productivity (NPP). We imposed an extreme drought (66% reduction in growing‐season precipitation) for 7 years in two semi‐arid grasslands, followed by a three‐year recovery. We quantified changes in several metrics of community trait composition and evaluated their relationships with NPP during and after drought. Prolonged drought shifted community composition in both grasslands from dominance by conservative perennial grasses to acquisitive annual forbs, and this shift persisted during recovery. Trait dispersion increased with prolonged drought in both grasslands, although recovery trajectories differed between grasslands. Communities characterized by more acquisitive strategies or greater trait dispersion showed lower productivity sensitivity to drought, likely because annual forbs, for example, escape drought, while greater trait dispersion provided functional insurance and niche complementarity within the community. These results advance our understanding of plant drought responses and highlight the importance of acquisitive strategies in grassland resistance and recovery from extreme, prolonged drought.

title: Beyond unseen entities: Auditable cold-start evaluation for drug interaction prediction
content:
by Xiaoqing Ru, Yansu Wang, Quan Zou, Mengting Niu

Reliable generalization is essential for deploying drug–drug interaction (DDI) and drug–target interaction (DTI) models in drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, and clinical decision support. However, strong performance on random splits or weakly constrained evaluations may not reflect how well a model generalizes to new drugs, targets, or deployment conditions. In pairwise prediction, test instances may still resemble training examples in molecular structure, sequence, or network context. Such overlap can inflate performance estimates and make interpolation appear to be extrapolation. In this Perspective, we argue that cold-start evaluation should be treated as an auditable deployment claim. We organize common evaluation settings by their source and scope of novelty, ranging from random splits and entity-disjoint protocols to structure-level, temporal, domain-disjoint, and many-domain evaluations. The L0–L5 framework clarifies which deployment claim each setting is designed to test. Coverage, overlap, and distance quantify the resulting train–test discrepancy. We further provide a practical checklist for leakage control, validation alignment, candidate-pair construction, and domain-level risk reporting. This Perspective clarifies the boundaries and evidential scope of cold-start evaluation, providing a common basis for interpreting and comparing results across DDI and DTI studies.

title: Estimating rates of SARS-CoV-2 lineage spread using graph spectra from genetic sequence data
content:
by Emma E. Goldberg, Michael D. Kupperman, Ruian Ke

The modern enormous scale of viral genomic data, as exemplified by SARS-CoV-2, presents unique opportunities for epidemic inference and real-time monitoring. A key challenge is to wade through the extremely large stream of sequence data in order to identify small subsets of sequences that may represent rapid population growth of newly emerged lineages. To address this challenge, we developed a new approach that combines techniques in graph theory and machine learning. We represent distances between small subsets of sequences as graph Laplacians and identify from them features of rapid population growth. From early sequence data collected in the US and the UK between 2021 and mid-2022, we identified two features—genetic diversity and graph connectivity—that allow us to reliably estimate growth rates of newly emerged lineages. To test our model, we used data collected from mid-2022 to end-2024 and accurately inferred the growth rates of lineages that appeared during this period. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for data collected in 2023 when the sequencing efforts were relatively high (thousands of sequences per day) in the US and the UK, our model correctly identified the most rapidly expanding lineages when they were still at low frequencies. Overall, our work provides a scalable and adaptable tool to estimate the growth rate of newly emerged SARS-CoV-2 lineages.

title: PhagoCyt enables isolation of Salmonella-containing phagosomes and mapping of host and bacteria remodelling of the intracellular niche
content:
by Ritika Chatterjee, José Luis Marin-Rubio, Francesca Romana Cianfanelli, Andrew Michael Frey, Benjamin Bernard Armando Raymond, Abeer Dannoura, Camila Valenzuela, Meihan Meng, Tiaan Heunis, Mengchun Li, Frances Sidgwick, Jost Enninga, Andrew Filby, Matthias Trost

Macrophages engulf pathogens into dynamic phagosomes, which many bacteria manipulate for survival. However, isolating pure pathogen-containing phagosomes remains challenging. Here, we developed a novel flow cytometry-based isolation and ultrasensitive proteomics approach to analyse phagosomal and bacterial proteomes from macrophages infected with wild-type (WT) Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STM) or a ΔphoP mutant at 30 min and 4 hours post-infection. Our approach provides higher throughput, requires lower cell numbers and quantifies more proteins than previous techniques. Our data reveals key host-pathogen interactions, showing induction of PhoP-dependent virulence factors and novel putative proteins that shape STM’s intracellular niche. Moreover, our data indicates that bacteria-containing phagosomes recruit mitochondrial membrane for production of reactive oxygen species. These findings provide new insights into Salmonella’s manipulation of phagosomal maturation and intracellular niche formation.

title: Vertebrate paired fins are specified by an ancient dorso-ventral patterning system
content:
by Rebecca E. Dale, Silke Berger, Sara Alaei, Marcus C. Davis, Frank J. Tulenko, Peter D. Currie

The origin of paired fins was a major event in early vertebrate history that fueled the adaptive radiation of the gnathostome clade. Evidence for the conservation of ancient regulatory systems between paired and median fins supports a model in which appendage-patterning mechanisms first evolved in the midline and were later redeployed to a new embryonic context, the flank. However, while paired fins and limbs are asymmetric along the dorsoventral (DV) axis, the equivalent axis does not exist in median fins, which are symmetric across the midline, raising questions of how DV patterning evolved. Here, we combine genetic tools in zebrafish with comparative expression analyses in representative ray-finned and cartilaginous fishes to show that a subset of limb DV patterning genes are expressed during median fin development. Using genetic lineage tracing of the canonical limb dorsalizing factor lmx1bb, we further demonstrate that, although lmx1bb-derived cells occupy distinct spatial domains across fin types, a subset of this lineage is fated to differentiate into fin ray osteoblasts in both paired and median fins. To test the potential conservation of regulatory modules across fin types, we generated a series of deletion mutants for two known lmx1b mouse limb enhancers, LARM1 and LARM2, that we show are partially conserved upstream of zebrafish lmx1bb. These experiments revealed that LARM function is essential for dorsoventral patterning of the paired pectoral and pelvic fins of zebrafish but is dispensable for formation of the unpaired dorsal and anal fins. Collectively, these data support the conservation of an ancient LARM-Lmx1b dorsal determination system in the paired fins of osteichthyans, challenge models proposing simple co-option of a pre-existing median fin gene regulatory network and suggest that the acquisition of this regulatory module may have been a key early step in the evolution of the paired fin DV patterning axis.

title: Midbrain somatostatin-expressing cells control pain-suppression during defensive states
content: In threatening situations, animals exhibit a broad range of behavioral and autonomic responses. As such, a crucial adaptive response is the inhibition of pain, which facilitates relevant defensive behaviors that promote survival. Whereas the structures and mechanisms involved in fear and pain behaviors are well documented, little is known about the precise neuronal mechanisms mediating the emotional regulation of endogenous pain-suppression. Here, we used a combination of behavioral, anatomical, optogenetic, and electrophysiological approaches to investigate, in male mice, the role of somatostatin-expressing cells in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray matter (SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells) in the control of analgesia induced during defensive states. Our data indicate that optogenetic inhibition of SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells promotes analgesia irrespective of animal defensive state. In contrast, optogenetic activation of long-range SST<sup>+</sup> vlPAG cells that project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) abolishes the analgesia mediated by fear behavior. title: Homogeneous network inference for subtype-stratified master regulator analysis in cancer
content: Master-regulator analysis of 34 TCGA tumour cohorts (cancer x molecular subtype; n between 27 and 562 tumours) requires one regulatory network per cohort. Mutual-information (MI) networks inferred with ARACNe3 are the usual choice, but they are not available for the smallest cohorts; filling the gap with correlation networks would mix two methods inside the very comparison between subtypes that the analysis is meant to make. We therefore infer every network with a single procedure, fixed-size Spearman regulons (FSR): rank correlation between regulator and target, a fixed effect-size threshold rho >= 0.2, the per-target data-processing-inequality (DPI) pruning implemented in corto, bootstrap support, and truncation to the 100 best-supported targets per regulator. We quantify what this choice concedes and what it provides, labelling each claim as a standard result, a heuristic, or an empirical result. Rank correlation is more powerful than the MI estimators we simulated for n < 200 but cannot see non-monotone dependence, which in a synthetic worst case costs at most about 0.05-0.10 of the master regulators recovered; the per-target DPI is a heuristic with a measurable disagreement rate with the MI-based one; and pairwise dependence is not direct interaction, for MI and correlation alike. Where both methods are feasible (n >= 95) they overlap in 0.7 of the top-20 regulators, the same as two filterings of the same ARACNe3 network, although the rank correlation of the full score vector shows a measurable method effect in the tail. Subsampling large real cohorts indicates that networks inferred from fewer than 60 tumours do not reliably reproduce their own cohort's master regulators, that 60-100 is a grey zone, and that a cancer-wide network does not rescue small subtypes. We present FSR as an adequate and uniform choice for multi-cohort analysis, not as a statistically superior one.

title: Dietary fibre combinations modulate gut microbiome composition and metabolic responses in zebrafish, with lasting effects on intestinal barrier gene expression
content: Food sources provide a complex mixture of dietary fibres, not a single type. Consuming a diverse range of these dietary fibre-containing foods is associated with health benefits. However, how the effects of combining dietary fibres translate across different biological levels remains poorly characterised. This study uses an integrated microbiome-metabolome analytical approach that combines 16S rRNA gene sequencing with metabolomic profiling of the intestine, brain and liver. Specifically, we examined the combined effects of apple pectin (AP) and cellulose (C) within the same diet, compared with their isolated effects, in adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Notably, the combined apple pectin and cellulose diet (APC) produced a microbiome composition that could not be predicted by simply adding the changes observed with each dietary fibre individually, indicating a significant non-additive interaction between the two dietary components, specifically a less-than-additive response in gut microbiome composition. The resulting community composition under the combined diet also more closely resembled that induced by apple pectin. We found that predicted microbial functional capabilities did not translate directly into quantified intestinal and brain short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations, nor did intestinal SCFA levels directly mirror those observed in the brain. Moreover, we used targeted qPCR gene expression analysis to assess responses to a subsequent saponin challenge after dietary fibre cessation, revealing a potentially protective effect on the intestinal barrier. Collectively, we show that dietary fibres within the same diet interact to shape the gut microbiome and do not act in isolation, leading to non-linear health ramifications for the host that may persist even after active consumption ends.

title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization
content: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii. Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii, a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-associated transcripts. A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
content: Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.

title: Characterization of Lactobacillus rhamnosus-Derived Extracellular Vesicles and Their Cellular Cytoprotective Effects Against Trimethylamine-Induced Oxidative Stress in Caco-2 Cells
content: Dietary trimethylamine (TMA) underwent gut microbiota-mediated catabolism and subsequent hepatic oxidation to generate trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a key metabolic factor linked to vascular and colorectal diseases. While the systemic effects of circulating TMAO were heavily investigated, the direct localized cellular interactions of its precursor, TMA, at the intestinal epithelial level required further elucidation. This study characterized extracellular vesicles isolated from Lactobacillus rhamnosus (Lr-EVs) and evaluated their cytoprotective potential in an in vitro human intestinal Caco-2 cell model under TMA-induced stress. Exposure to a high concentration of TMA (20 mM) significantly reduced Caco-2 viability to 78.8%, triggered intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and compromised tight junction integrity as observed via the disruption of Zonula Occludens-1 (ZO-1) alignment. Co-treatment with Lr-EVs (100-300 g/mL) counteracted this cellular toxicity, enhancing cell survival up to 172%. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that Lr-EVs suppressed the transcriptional upregulation of the pro-inflammatory gene IL-1{beta}, restored the expression of the metabolic regulator SIRT1, and stabilized transcript levels of key mitochondrial-encoded electron transport chain genes (ND6, CYTB, CO1, and ATP6). Additionally, Lr-EVs exhibited intrinsic radical scavenging activities in cell-free ABTS and DPPH assays. These preliminary in vitro findings demonstrated that Lr-EVs mitigated TMA-induced cellular injury, oxidative stress, and junctional disruption at the transcriptomic level, supporting further investigation of probiotic-derived EVs as prospective cell-free functional ingredients.

title: Novel viral diversity and geographic structuring in the New Zealand West Coast blackfly (Austrosimulium ungulatum)
content: Background Vector-borne diseases represent a major global public health burden, with climate change, land-use change and increasing human activity altering arthropod vector distributions and creating opportunities for infectious disease emergence. In Aotearoa New Zealand, insects commonly referred to as "sandflies" are blackflies belonging to the family Simuliidae. The West Coast blackfly, Austrosimulium ungulatum, is an endemic, human-biting species abundant throughout the South Island, yet its associated viral diversity remains largely unexplored. Methods Here, we used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the virome of the West Coast blackfly and investigate patterns of viral diversity and community composition across geographical and environmental gradients. A total of 425 blackflies were collected from 19 locations spanning approximately 187 km. Results We identified 94 viral sequences across 16 orders and six phyla, all of which were putatively novel viruses. These included divergent lineages within families containing recognised vertebrate and arthropod pathogens, such as the Rhabdoviridae and Orthomyxoviridae. Viral community composition varied among sampling locations, but no significant associations were detected between land-use categories and viral diversity or community composition. In contrast, we revealed a weak but significant positive correlation between geographical distance and viral community dissimilarity, suggesting some degree of spatial structuring across the sampling range. Conclusions This study provides the first metatranscriptomic characterisation of the virome associated with the endemic West Coast blackfly, revealing substantial previously undescribed viral diversity and providing insights into the geographical distribution of arthropod-associated viral communities.

title: Structural basis of virion assembly in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis-infecting mycobacteriophage SWU1
content: The rising threat of drug-resistant tuberculosis has renewed interest in bacteriophage therapy as an urgently needed alternative. Rational engineering of these viruses, however, requires an atomic-level understanding of virion architecture. Mycobacteriophage SWU1 belongs to subcluster A2, one of the few mycobacteriophage lineages known to infect Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis). Using single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we resolved essentially the entire SWU1 virion architecture by localized reconstruction of four modules, the capsid, portal vertex, tail and baseplate, at resolutions of 3.62 [A], 3.51 [A], 3.70 [A] and 3.22 [A], respectively. The T=7 capsid comprises 415 copies of an HK97-fold major capsid protein and lacks any decoration protein in density. The 12-fold portal reconciles its C5-C12 mismatch with the capsid vertex through defined, non-equivalent subunit contacts. The baseplate carries a 13-fold tail-fiber ring on a 6-fold hub, a geometry without precedent among characterized phages, established here by symmetry-free reconstruction. These findings provide the critical insights into the assembly and infection of SWU1, laying a structural foundation for the future optimization of phage-based anti-TB therapeutics.

title: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States
content: Food-producing animals are a focus of One Health approaches to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as reservoirs of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). We hypothesized that microbial composition, ARGs profiles, and mobile genetic element (MGE) profiles would differ by operation size and animal age group. Fecal samples from 162 cows and calves were combined into 54 composite samples, each comprising three animals of the same age group. Across operation sizes, Bacillota (51.4-64.9%), Bacteroidota (12.0-17.3%), Pseudomonadota (10.3-16.5%), and Actinomycetota (3.3-10.9%) were predominant phyla. Alpha diversity did not differ among operation sizes; however, cows exhibited greater observed richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity than calves (all P < 0.001). Microbial composition did not differ significantly among operation sizes (PERMANOVA, R{superscript 2} = 0.065, P = 0.609) but differed significantly between cows and calves (R{superscript 2} = 0.200, P < 0.001). Seventy-five ARGs representing 14 resistance classes were identified. Normalized ARG hit rates were higher in small operations (0.444) than in medium (0.278) and large operations (0.222; P = 0.088), whereas calves exhibited a higher estimated marginal mean normalized ARG hit rate than cows (0.383 vs. 0.247 hits/million reads; P < 0.001). Of 1,054 curated ARG hits, 23.9% occurred on predicted plasmid contigs, 0.9% on predicted viral contigs, and 7.1% on contigs containing insertion sequences. Overall findings demonstrate differences in fecal microbiome diversity and ARG abundance between cows and calves and indicate that predicted plasmids are associated with a notable proportion of ARG hits in Florida beef cow-calf operations.

title: Mucin promotes pneumococcal colonization via autolysis suppression and tryptophan-mediated immune modulation
content: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a leading human respiratory pathogen, yet its success depends not on disease but on its ability to persist as an asymptomatic colonizer of the nasopharynx. The nasopharyngeal mucosa is lined with mucus, whose heavily O-glycosylated mucin proteins are the most abundant macromolecules in the pneumococcal natural niche. While mucus is canonically viewed as a host defense barrier, we found that mucin actively reprograms pneumococcal physiology to promote colonization through two distinct mechanisms. First, mucin suppresses pneumococcal autolysis by specifically inhibiting the enzymatic activity of the major autolysin LytA, prolonging bacterial survival and restricting release of the cholesterol-dependent cytotoxin pneumolysin, thereby reducing host cell damage. Second, mucin induces de novo biosynthesis and extracellular release of tryptophan, an essential amino acid that humans cannot synthesize and that serves as a substrate for host immunomodulatory pathways. Tryptophan biosynthesis was critical for pneumococcal survival against macrophage killing, and its disruption abolished both colonization and invasive disease. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that tryptophan biosynthesis enables the pneumococcus to survive a bactericidal macrophage state while preventing macrophage transition to proliferative tissue repair. Together, these findings reveal that mucin is not merely a barrier but an active signal that reprograms the pneumococcus toward a persistent, host-tolerant state, identifying a distinctive repertoire of colonization mechanisms that allow a virulent respiratory pathogen to sustain long-term asymptomatic carriage in its human reservoir.

title: Host availability, climate and pupal-stage ecology shape the predicted environmental suitability of the New World screwworm across Central and South America
content: Background: The New World screwworm, Cochliomyia hominivorax, causes primary myiasis in warm-blooded vertebrates. Its recent resurgence in Central America has renewed the need for spatial tools that identify environmentally suitable areas and surveillance gaps. Most previous distribution models have emphasized climate and livestock, whereas ecological constraints acting during the free-living pupal stage have rarely been incorporated. Methods: We compiled 2,461 georeferenced occurrence reports from the literature across Central and South America and linked them to climate, livestock density, forest cover and superficial soil predictors. Four sequential (nested) logistic models quantified the incremental contribution of predictor blocks, compared using likelihood-ratio tests, AIC and discrimination metrics. Logistic regression and Random Forest were then compared using five-fold spatial block cross-validation, which we treat as the primary measure of generalisation, and an independent municipality-level 70:30 train-test split. Variable importance was assessed using Random Forest Mean Decrease Accuracy together with partial-dependence profiles. Because presence and pseudo-absence classes were balanced before fitting, model outputs are interpreted as relative environmental suitability rather than absolute probability of occurrence. Results: The literature database represented 2,589 infected hosts, dominated by cattle, pigs, dogs and humans. Across the sequential models, AUC increased from 0.780 for climate alone to 0.898 with livestock density, 0.908 with forest cover and 0.918 with superficial soil properties; the increment attributable to the soil block ({Delta}AUC = 0.010) was smaller than the between-fold variability observed under spatial cross-validation (SD 0.049) and is therefore reported as suggestive rather than established. Sheep and horse density and cold-quarter soil temperature showed the highest Mean Decrease Accuracy values, while silt texture ranked above cattle density and forest cover. Under spatial block cross-validation Random Forest was markedly more stable than the GLM (mean AUC 0.926 {+/-} 0.049 versus 0.814 {+/-} 0.157) and was retained as the final model. On the independent municipality-level test set it achieved AUC 0.981, TSS 0.824, sensitivity 0.850 and specificity 0.972, values we regard as optimistic relative to the spatially blocked estimates. Predicted suitability was highest across Central America and parts of northern and tropical South America. Conclusions: C. hominivorax occurrence was associated with interacting climatic, host and landscape conditions. Superficial soil variables added a small, biologically interpretable signal consistent with constraints acting during pupation, but one that lies within the uncertainty of our spatial validation and requires confirmation with independent data. The maps estimate relative environmental suitability rather than infection incidence, and are intended to identify areas where surveillance could be strengthened rather than to guide control operations directly.

title: Positive relationships between interspecific association strength and elevational range overlap highlight the role of facilitation in community assembly
content: The interplay of abiotic conditions and biotic interactions determines individual species' ranges, and by extension therefore, community assembly. To date, studies have focused predominantly on abiotic filtering (e.g., temperature) and agonistic interactions (e.g., competition) as potential drivers of community assembly; the role of facilitation in setting geographical range limits and structuring communities remains unclear. We tested how participation in compositionally distinct modules of facilitative networks of interactions in mixed-species bird flocks (MSFs) influenced interspecific elevational range overlaps across a 2000m elevational gradient in the hyperdiverse Eastern Himalaya. Species that participated in MSFs had higher average elevational range overlap compared with MSF non-participants. Positive correlations between pairwise association strength in MSFs and elevational range overlap were found for all MSF modules. We highlight the potential role of facilitation in determining species co-occurrence patterns and assembling communities across large spatial gradients.

title: Influence of Soluble and Mineral Sources of Cobalt on Methanogenesis and Growth in Methanosarcina barkeri Fusaro and Methanococcus maripaludis S2
content:
Mode of methanogenesis and sulphur source affected cobalt (availability and biosynthetic demand in cultures of Methanosarcina barkeri Fusaro and Methanococcus maripaludis S2. Both strains reductively dissolved cobaltoan pyrite, (Co,Fe)S2, as a source of iron, Co and sulphur and assimilated the mobilized Co as cobalamide cofactors. These findings provide insight into factors that influence Co demands in methanogens and show that mineral sources of Co that prevail under sulphidic conditions commonly inhabited by methanogens are bioavailable.

ABSTRACT
Cobalt (Co) is a required component of cofactors and coenzymes in all life and has a pronounced role in the one carbon metabolism of methanogens. However, methanogens often inhabit sulphidic environments where Co precipitates and is incorporated into low solubility mineral phases, such as pyrite (FeS2). Here, we initially examined the influence of Co availability on the growth kinetics of (1) Methanosarcina barkeri with different methanogenesis substrates and (2) Methanococcus maripaludis with different sulphur sources. We then investigated Co acquisition from cobaltoan pyrite [(Co,Fe)S2]. Co demand was highest in M. barkeri grown on methanol/acetate relative to hydrogen/carbon dioxide or methanol only and in M. maripaludis grown with sulphide relative to cysteine or cysteine/thiosulphate. Methanol/acetate‐grown M. barkeri and formate‐grown M. maripaludis grew with (Co,Fe)S2 as well as with soluble sources of Co, Fe and S. Both strains required direct contact to reduce and solubilize Fe and S from (Co,Fe)S2. Further, M. barkeri grown with (Co,Fe)S2 produced an equal amount of cobamides relative to cells provided with soluble Co, Fe, and S. These findings indicate that the availability of methanogenesis substrates and sulphur sources influence Co requirements for methanogens and that these organisms can acquire Co, Fe and S from (Co,Fe)S2.

title: Plant hydraulic traits regulating productivity and drought resistance in boreal crops
content:
Plant hydraulic traits regulating productivity and drought resistance in boreal crops
Hui Tang, Samuli Launiainen, Julius Vira, Liisa Kulmala, Taru Palosuo, Hermanni Aaltonen, Olli Nevalainen, Istem Fer, Henriikka Vekuri, Jari-Pekka Nousu, Mika Korkiakoski, and Jari Liski

title: Increased Hydrological Connectivity Does Not Always Lead to Increased Nutrient Removal Potential in a Coastal River Delta
content:
Abstract
Coastal river deltas can act as important nitrate sinks, reducing nutrient loads that contribute to coastal hypoxia. Their removal capacity depends not only on local biogeochemical conditions but also on the transport pathways of nutrients through the delta. Nutrient transport to key processing areas, the deltaic islands, is governed by hydrological connectivity, which varies with discharge and seasonal vegetation. Most estimates of delta‐scale denitrification rely on up‐scaled field measurements that do not explicitly account for these transport dynamics. A key knowledge gap is how denitrification potential differs between seasons of peak connectivity and peak vegetation. This study asked whether nitrate removal is greater during periods of high connectivity, when more particles enter high‐processing areas, or low connectivity, when increased vegetation may extend particle residence times. More broadly, we examined whether removal is controlled by transport to reactive areas or processing efficiency within them. To address this question, we coupled a nutrient uptake module with a Lagrangian particle tracking model and applied it to two hydrodynamic simulations calibrated for spring and fall conditions in Louisiana's Wax Lake Delta. Our results show that increased connectivity does not enhance denitrification. Instead, high flows create a flushing effect that limits removal despite greater access to reactive areas. Denitrification is enhanced by prolonged exposure times in fall, independent of seasonal increases in reaction rates. Future delta‐scale denitrification estimates should prioritize exposure‐time estimation, as refining first‐order decay rates adds limited information and water‐extent upscaling fails to capture seasonal hydrodynamic variability.

title: Fine‐Scale Covariability of Sea Surface Temperature and Winds Across an Oceanic Front: Part I‐Observational Evidence From Two S‐MODE Cases
content:
Abstract
Air–sea coupling at scales of 1–10 km plays a critical role in regulating ocean–atmosphere exchanges but remains poorly characterized due to observational limitations. In this study, we examine fine‐scale sea surface temperature (SST)‐wind covariability using collocated airborne SST and 10‐m wind vector observations from two targeted cases during the Sub‐Mesoscale ocean dynamics experiment (S‐MODE): 25 October 2021 and 24 October 2022. The airborne SST fields are calibrated using in situ observations, corrected for cross‐track scalloping artifacts, and validated against satellite SST products. In both cases, coherent spatial relationship between SST and wind speed is characterized by enhanced winds over warmer SSTs and reduced winds over cooler SSTs. Atmospheric responses are found to lag underlying SST gradients by approximately 2–7 km in the downwind direction, consistent with the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) adjustment processes. Cross‐frontal contrasts, perturbation‐based regressions, and the relationship between wind divergence and alongwind SST gradients provide complementary evidence of SST‐wind covariability under the sampled frontal conditions. Comparisons with an idealized MABL response model further support a stability‐driven mechanism linking SST to near‐surface wind variability. The estimated coupling slopes and lag distances are specific to the two selected cases and should not be interpreted as statistically representative of all S‐MODE conditions. These findings provide observational evidence of km‐scale wind–SST coupling and highlight the value of high‐resolution, simultaneous SST and wind measurements for investigating frontal air‐sea interactions.

title: Fine‐Scale Covariability of Sea Surface Temperature and Winds Across an Oceanic Front: Part II‐ Synergistic Insights From SAR and Multi‐Platform Observations
content:
Abstract
Atmospheric response to sharp sea surface temperature (SST) fronts is a key element of air‐sea interaction at mesoscales (1–10 km), yet it remains difficult to examine because truly collocated, high‐resolution observations of SST and near‐surface winds are rare. In this study, we take advantage of multi‐platform observations collected on 24 October 2022 in Sub‐Mesoscale Ocean Dynamics Experiment experimental region to examine the marine atmospheric boundary layer (MABL) adjustment across a sharp SST front. Near‐surface winds are stronger over the warm side of the front and weaker over the cold side, consistent with stratification‐dependent modulation of turbulent mixing in the MABL. Changes of SST versus wind speed across the front center line are coherent, with sharper contrast resolved at finer spatial spacing. Concurrent Sentinel‐1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images reveals variability in MABL structures, from boundary layer roll dominance over the colder region toward mixed states with cell over warmer surface. Such a pattern transition is consistent with reduced near‐surface stratification and enhanced mixing across SST front with wind blowing from cold to warm patch. These results demonstrate the utility of combining SST, winds, and SAR roughness to diagnose fine‐scale air‐sea coupling and provide a process‐based template for exploiting future collocated observations, including those anticipated from European Space Agency’s Harmony mission.

title: Life Cycle Complexity Shapes Parasite Sharing Amongst Migratory and Resident Hosts
content:
ABSTRACT
Migratory animals are potentially important parasite dispersers. However, understanding the impact of host migration on parasite distributions is challenging because variation in parasite life histories can mediate dispersal potential. Furthermore, studies of parasite dispersal via host migration often compare parasites in different species of migrant and resident hosts, despite differences in host phylogeny, ecology, and exposure history, which can complicate ascertaining the impact of migration. The Tasmanian population of silvereye Zosterops lateralis lateralis) exhibits partial migration. Some members of the population overwinter on the Australian mainland, where they co‐occur with residents of another silvereye subspecies (Z. l. cornwalli). Utilising targeted PCR, metabarcoding and high‐throughput sequencing, we characterise a range of parasite genera from blood and faecal samples in Tasmanian resident, migrant and mainland resident birds. Greater parasite richness was documented in migrant individuals, possibly reflecting exposure to varied parasite faunas at stopovers or during overwintering. The increased richness was primarily driven by parasites with simple life cycles. Reduced sharing of parasites with complex life cycles amongst migratory and resident host populations may be explained by ecological constraints in establishing transmission, such as vector or secondary host availability. Our study exemplifies the utility of molecular methods for characterising multi‐parasite systems and makes use of a single host species to provide insights on patterns of parasite distributions that result from migratory movements. Knowing how parasite life histories constrain or promote dispersal via regular host migration will be essential for predicting future patterns of pathogen dispersal under climate change and shifting migratory regimes.

title: Demographic Recovery Masks Matrilineal Lineage Compression in the Chinese Alligator
content:
ABSTRACT
Demographic recovery is often used as evidence of conservation success, yet population growth does not necessarily restore maternally inherited genetic diversity. The Critically Endangered Chinese alligator (Alligator sinensis) has increased numerically under captive breeding, but contemporary maternal‐lineage representation remains poorly resolved. Here, we assembled control‐region‐excluded mitochondrial genomes from 356 individuals across six groups (F1, F2, F3, F4, wild and ZJ). Mitochondrial nucleotide diversity was extremely low (π = 5.41 × 10−5). Although 16 haplotypes were detected, 88.2% of sampled individuals carried only two dominant haplotypes, revealing pronounced matrilineal lineage compression. These findings show that demographic recovery can coexist with restricted contemporary representation of maternal lineages, underscoring that census growth alone does not constitute matrilineal recovery. Monitoring maternal lineages alongside nuclear genomic variation and census size can therefore provide a more complete assessment of conservation recovery.

Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides
content:
by Elizaveta A. Bogdanova, Timofei F. Lukianov, Artem V. Chernukhin, Alexey K. Shaytan

Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI – a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences. This ensures efficient processing not only of canonical peptides but also of non-canonical modifications, cyclic structures, and peptide-like small molecules. We also created an original dataset for model training integrating data from public databases and relevant scientific publications. The algorithm simultaneously predicts key parameters including membrane permeability (Caco-2 and PAMPA penetration), distribution and excretion (half-life, clearance, volume of distribution), as well as general and specific toxicity profiles (neurotoxicity, hemolytic activity). A key innovation of the study is the integration of functional pharmacokinetic scoring. The model not only predicts ADMET values but also calculates an adaptive suitability rating for a compound in the context of its specific biological activity. We have conducted a comparative analysis of various data encoding strategies implementing a stack of models ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern transformers and language models in classification modes. Results from testing on independent test sets demonstrate high prediction accuracy and interpretability of features making Pepti-DrugPhAI a powerful tool for more robust selection of promising peptide drug candidates. All data and the code are available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EABogdanova/Pepti-DrugPhAI.

title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics
content:
by Mengyi Yan, Xiaoxiu Tan, Zhenhao Liu, Siwen Zhang, Yiwen Du, Hong Li, Lanming Chen, Lu Xie

Spatial omics enables analysis of tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, but most spatial tools are optimized for transcriptomics and poorly suited to proteomics data. We developed Sphinx, an R package providing a comprehensive workflow for spatial proteomics, including preprocessing, cell annotation, adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Importantly, it introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and incorporates computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, enabling robust neighborhood modeling. Notably, Sphinx offers improved computational efficiency and scalability. Across lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen datasets, Sphinx robustly identifies cell types and spatial functional units, including tertiary lymphoid structures. We also explored the application of Sphinx to paired high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, illustrating its potential applicability. Sphinx provides a flexible and efficient framework for spatial proteomics, enabling robust characterization of spatial organization and tissue microenvironments.

title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity
content:
by Pablo Sanchez-Martin, Irene Elices, Alicia Garrido-Peña, Carlos Garcia-Saura, Rafael Levi, Francisco B. Rodriguez, Pablo Varona

In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles. Our results help understand the mechanisms underlying the autonomous cycle-by-cycle sequential coordination and the relationships between intervals from consecutive cycles when a slow modulatory action establishes a common trend across the rhythm.

title: An antigen-specific protein language model guides CDR optimization for antibody design
content:
by Faisal Bin Ashraf, Karen Paco, Sanaz Zebardast, Zihao Zhang, Ryan Mooney, Christian J. Dávila Ojeda, Mariana Paco Mendivil, Rashid M. Alam, Eva Chen, Iraneus Ogu, Jordan A. Lay, Tristan Y. Yang, Fernando L. Barroso da Silva, Malkiat Johal, Ilya Tolstorukov, Matthew H. Sazinsky, Animesh Ray, Stefano Lonardi

The capacity of an antibody to recognize and bind an antigen with high specificity and strength (i.e., its binding affinity) is a key determinant in the design and optimization of neutralizing antibodies against pathogenic targets. Here we introduce Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) that predicts the binding affinity of an antibody against a target peptide within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Cross-validation results shows that that Ab-Affinity outperforms other PLM-based affinity predictors when evaluated on a held-out validation and independent test sets. When integrated with a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing for sequence diversification and fitness optimization, Ab-Affinity enables the generation of candidate antibodies exhibiting over 100-fold improvement in predicted binding affinity relative to its parental (natural) antibody. More broadly, antibodies designed with Ab-Affinity attain higher predicted binding affinities than those produced by alternative mutational strategies, yielding synthetic antibodies with favorable predicted biophysical characteristics. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations for the strongest synthetic candidates indicate enhanced interactions and increased stability with the target peptide epitope within the spike protein. Experimental validation in vitro for a top-ranked candidate reveals an apparent increase in binding relative to its parental antibody. All model weights, source code, and analysis pipelines are publicly released to allow full reproducibility.

title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq
content:
by Xiaodong Zeng, Jingwen Zhang, Shan Li, Haohua Wang

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics
content:
by Sebastian Manuel Geli, Juan Manuel Monti, Adrián Ponce-Alvarez, Gustavo Deco, Yonatan Sanz Perl

A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region’s future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation–dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain’s memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models
content:
by Theresa M. Pauli, Theresa von Heyl, Beate Rieblinger, Sabrina Teresa Schleibinger, Wei Liang, Antonia Schmauser, Mithuoshni Arullmoli, Paul Derrer, Anika Eckstein, Sirradu Jagana, Camila Gatti Corrêa, Krzysztof Flisikowski, Tatiana Flisikowska, Benjamin Schusser

Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human–animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

title: A new asymmetry, an old toolkit: An emerging developmental enigma in appendage evolution
content:
by Caroline Schwaner, Tetsuya Nakamura

Dorsoventral polarity is a key feature of paired appendages, yet its evolutionary origin is enigmatic as median fins, which predate paired appendages, are symmetric. A new PLOS Biology study shows lmx1b is dorsal in paired fin mesenchyme but posterior in median fins, implying genetic rewiring of an ancient toolkit. Dorsoventral polarity is a key feature of paired appendages, yet its evolutionary origin is enigmatic as median fins, which predate paired appendages, are symmetric. A new study shows that lmx1b is dorsal in paired fin mesenchyme but posterior in median fins, implying genetic rewiring of an ancient toolkit.

title: The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry sequentially drives invasion and host-parasite interface formation
content:
by Allison Cohen, Tim Bergner, Amandine Guérin, Maryse Lebrun, Michael Laue, Christian Klotz, Boris Striepen

The apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease in young children. Within the intestinal epithelium, Cryptosporidium establishes a unique intracellular niche in the apical brush border of enterocytes. A structurally complex interface between host and parasite acts as a holdfast and enables protein and metabolite transport. How the parasite invades its host cell and builds the interface is poorly understood. Here, we reveal parasite invasion with high temporal and spatial resolution using rigorous molecular markers. We find that sequential discharge of specialized secretory organelles anchors the parasite within the host prior to internalization. The single Cryptosporidium rhoptry persists beyond its initial pre-invasion discharge, acting as a conduit for the secretion of multiple waves of effector proteins. Ultimately, the rhoptry membrane gives rise to the feeder organelle that separates host from parasite cytoplasm. These findings lead us to propose a mechanistic model of Cryptosporidium invasion and intracellular parasitism.

title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval
content: Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2–4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding–retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine’s role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

title: Lithospheric‐Scale Martian Tectonic Deformation: Defining the Strength Profile Through Parameter Testing
content:
Abstract
We incorporate recent data constraints from the 2018 InSight mission into two rheology yielding mechanisms to calculate the plastic (brittle) and viscous (ductile) yield stresses for 30 potential lithospheric scenarios of the Martian lithosphere. Through these calculations, we produce estimates for the depth of the transition from brittle to ductile deformation for each scenario. We systematically test 7 parameter groups and find that the most common result is a strong brittle lithosphere that produces a deep (>150 km) brittle‐ductile transition (BDT), while scenarios with Moho temperatures ≥700 K produce shallow, crustal‐scale BDTs. Finally, we present our reference calculation as a 2‐D lithospheric numerical model under horizontal shortening and show the resulting deformation to produce regional‐scale surface faults controlled by a deep lithosphere‐scale thrust. Our findings have broad implications, demonstrating the potential for deep, brittle faulting hidden beneath the Martian surface.

title: Consistent Sea‐Level and Energy Budget Residuals Suggest Enhanced Deep‐Ocean Heat Uptake Since the Mid‐2010s
content:
Abstract
The deep ocean (>2,000 m) comprises ∼50% of the total ocean volume and is crucial in Earth's climate system, yet its warming remains uncertain owing to limited observations. We revisit the recently reported non‐closure of the global mean sea‐level (GMSL) budget and show that, despite instrumental corrections, the budget residual has increased since the mid‐2010s. Furthermore, the contribution of ocean heat uptake above 2,000 m to Earth's energy imbalance (EEI) has declined from approximately 80% to nearly 50% after the mid‐2010s, leaving a larger fraction of the EEI to be accounted for by deep ocean and other components of the climate system. When the GMSL budget residual was converted into the deep‐ocean heat uptake, the total heat uptake is consistent with the corresponding EEI estimates within uncertainty. These results demonstrate quantitative consistency between the GMSL and EEI budget residuals and suggest that deep‐ocean heat uptake have increased since the mid‐2010s.

title: Predictability Limit of RMM Index Modulated by Diverse ENSO Events
content:
Abstract
The Madden‐Julian Oscillation (MJO), a crucial source of subseasonal predictability, experiences El Niño‐Southern Oscillation (ENSO) modulation whose impacts vary by event type. Using an analog‐based methodology that incorporates a history of dynamical system evolution and epsilon‐based neighborhoods, we quantify how Eastern‐Pacific (EP) and Central‐Pacific (CP) ENSO events distinctly regulate the predictability limit of the real‐time multivariate MJO (RMM) index. Results unravel a remarkable 9‐day predictability advantage during EP La Niña over EP El Niño, attributable to stronger amplitude and prolonged persistence of initial signals, particularly during RMM phases 1–2 and 7–8. In contrast, how CP ENSO modulates the predictability is phase‐dependent, owing to the balance between MJO signal strength and atmospheric high‐frequency noises. Therefore, the overall predictability of the RMM index remains similar across CP ENSO states. These findings underscore the need to jointly account for the initial RMM phase and ENSO type in improving subseasonal forecasting.

title: Evaluation of Gridded Data Sets for Representing Precipitation Event Properties Across 20 U.S. Gulf Coast Locations
content:
Abstract
The skill of gridded sub‐daily precipitation products to represent rainfall event properties remains uncertain. Here, we evaluate four gauge‐influenced (AORC, MRMS, MSWEP, and Stage IV) and four gauge‐independent (PERSIANN, IMERG, ERA5, and MERRA2) products using 128,141 events across 20 U.S. Gulf Coast locations during 2015–2024. We assess event intensity (minimum, average, and maximum), duration, and volume. Rainfall volume is generally represented better than intensity and duration, particularly for moderate and major events, partly because of compensation between underestimated intensity and overestimated duration. MRMS and Stage IV best reproduce average and maximum intensities among gauge‐influenced products, while PERSIANN performs best among gauge‐independent products, suggesting potential value for intensity estimation where gauges are sparse. Minimum intensity is poorly represented by most products, highlighting difficulty in capturing weak intermittent rainfall. Overall, accurate event volume can mask distorted event structure, highlighting the importance of evaluating various event properties when selecting gridded precipitation products.
