title: Quantifying Bulk Silica of Felsic and Mafic Lithologies on Mars
content:
Abstract
On Earth, silica‐rich volcanism is typically associated with convergent plate boundaries, yet Mars, a stagnant‐lid body, also hosts regions with silicic lithologies. Here, we introduce a novel approach to directly estimate bulk silica (SiO2 wt.%) using multispectral data and machine learning. Our results reveal that an exposed pluton within a crater in Syrtis Major exhibits notably higher silica concentrations (62–83 wt.%) compared to the volcanic rocks of Nili Patera (60–72 wt.%). This observation suggests the presence of dacitic lithologies in Nili Patera and rhyolitic compositions in Syrtis Major, indicating that Mars may have experienced multi‐stage magmatic crystallization processes akin to Earth. Furthermore, Nili Fossae displays diurnal variations in silica, with higher values in the afternoon and lower values in the evening (35–55 wt.% SiO2), consistent with ultramafic bedrock overlain by silica‐enriched dust. These quantitative estimates will enable quantification and mapping of various lithologies and provide insight into its compositional evolution.

title: Rare Multiple Ionospheric Disturbances Observed During the Artemis‐II Lunar Flyby Voyage
content:
Abstract
The total electron content observations during the Artemis‐II Lunar mission revealed rare ionospheric perturbations occurring at three different occasions. The launch at 2235 UT on 1 April 2026 from Kennedy Space Center induced shock‐acoustic and gravity wave modulations. Subsequent Apogee Raise Maneuver (ARM) performed at 0023 UT on 2 April triggered shock waves and much intense large‐scale disturbances that elongated ∼50° longitude across North America. The third orbital maneuver conducted as part of trans‐Lunar injection (TLI) at 2349 UT on 2 April, yielded similar, but weaker large‐scale perturbations. This is the first time a single space mission producing such multiple ionospheric disturbances over the same region. The observed amplitudes suggest that despite releasing large exhaust energy, the disturbances during the rocket ascent produced weaker perturbations, whereas fewer amounts of direct energy deposition at ionosphere altitudes during ARM and TLI yielded up to 9 times intense perturbations elongated along the trajectory.

title: Fault‐Related Structure Revealed From Surface‐Wave Attenuation Using Distributed Acoustic Sensing on Dark Fiber
content:
Abstract
Blind fault mapping requires dense observations over large areas, and distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) provides a viable solution using dark fibers. Seismic attenuation is sensitive to fault‐related structure but relies on reliable amplitude measurements. In DAS data, amplitudes are distorted by non‐attenuation effects, including non‐uniform coupling and small‐scale heterogeneity, limiting their direct use for attenuation imaging. Here, we propose an attenuation imaging method based on ambient noise cross‐correlation functions, in which double virtual shot gathers are used to separate attenuation‐related and non‐attenuation‐related amplitude contributions. Using 6 hr of noise data, we obtain an attenuation coefficient profile along a 7.2‐km DAS array with sub‐kilometer resolution. The image reveals three strong‐attenuation zones, two of which are likely associated with fault‐related structures characterized by strong scattered waves, while the third is more likely associated with a low‐velocity structure. These results highlight the potential of DAS‐based ambient‐noise attenuation imaging for large‐scale, high‐resolution fault exploration.

Parsimonious Creatures: Building Gene Regulatory Networks Robust to Somatic Evolution
content: For early multicellular life to have formed and maintained cellular organization, preventing loss of controlled cell replication due to somatic evolution was of critical importance, and remains important to this day for control of cancer. We study how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) can be designed to slow the divergence of somatic clonal lineages in the context of early multicellular life. We model the mutation of GRNs within simplified 12-celled organisms we term "parsimonious creatures", who must replicate from a single cell to 12 cells and then prevent replication past 12 cells to maximize fitness. We found two minimal motifs can achieve these goals, but both are prone to breakdown through somatic evolution: The feedforward motif, which is loosely regulating but relatively robust, and the simple step motif, which uses strong interactions and feedback to form memoryless ultrasensitivity, but is fragile. These simple motifs may be duplicated to form redundant networks via one of two structures: averaging redundancy, which averages multiple sources of information, and min redundancy, which adopts the most conservative source. Averaging redundancy uniformly slows somatic evolution, while min redundancy stalls somatic evolution until neutral mutations accumulate. Either may be superior dependent on life history. However, averaging redundancy slowly increases fitness as the network becomes larger, but large min redundancy networks eventually become "paralyzed", increasing the probability of senescence and reducing fitness. These GRN designs are idealized, yet provide imperfect solutions with fundamental tradeoffs, offering insight as to why somatic evolution remains an incompletely solved problem for multicellular life.

title: Within-host evolution of an avirulent Salmonella vaccine strain reveals regulatory tuning of virulence functionality without loss of function
content: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) relies on a costly epithelial invasion program encoded in Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1) to overcome microbiota-mediated colonization resistance. Because SPI-1 expression is a cooperative trait in which a minority of invasive SPI-1ON cells benefits the wider bacterial population, inflammatory infection models readily select for permanently avirulent "cheater" mutants defective in SPI-1 function. However, while frequently observed during acute infection, isolates from persistent human NTS infection rarely exhibit obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function mutations, raising the question of whether SPI-1 contributes to bacterial fitness beyond induction of acute intestinal inflammation and tissue persistence. Here, we addressed this question using a metabolically attenuated yet epithelial-invasive auxotrophic Salmonella serovar Typhimurium (STm) vaccine strain (STmAux) that persistently colonizes the murine intestine without causing overt inflammatory pathology or tissue infection while retaining SPI-1-dependent host interaction and immunogenicity. Following within-host evolution for up to five years, STmAux populations did not accumulate classical hilD or other obvious SPI-1 loss-of-function cheater mutants. Instead, parallel evolution repeatedly targeted the BarA/SirA two-component regulatory system, closely mirroring previous observations in persistent human NTS infections. Functional analyses demonstrated that evolved barA and sirA alleles tune rather than abolish SPI-1 function by sharply reducing the proportion of SPI-1ON cells while preserving their individual epithelial invasion competence. Reconstructed in a prototrophic strain background, early evolved isolates retained full intestinal and systemic virulence in vivo despite exhibiting strongly reduced SPI-1ON frequencies in vitro. Remarkably, identical sirA mutant alleles also emerged in a hilD-deficient strain background, indicating that selection for these adaptive variants is not contingent on canonical HilD-dependent SPI-1 activation. During prolonged evolution, additional mutations accumulated that were associated with loss of systemic virulence despite preservation of epithelial invasiveness, suggesting subsequent adaptation affecting host-interaction pathways beyond SPI-1-mediated virulence. Together, these findings identify regulatory tuning of the BarA/SirA control network as a conserved evolutionary trajectory during prolonged NTS persistence. Rather than favoring classical cheater-driven loss of virulence functions, long-term adaptation preserves substantial SPI-1-dependent host interaction while reducing the proportion of phenotypically virulent SPI-1ON cells.

title: Structural signatures of salinity adaptation in Microviricetes capsids
content: Phages, like their bacterial hosts, have evolved to proliferate across the full range of environments on Earth, but the specific amino acid residues that underlie their environmental adaptations remain elusive. Here, we developed a computational framework that uses structure-based multiple sequence alignments, a random forest classifier, and a phylogeny-aware regression model to find amino acid residues linked to specific environments. Applying this framework to public metagenomic data, we analyzed 1,110 Microviricetes major capsid proteins (MCPs) from the lake and ocean biomes, and found that ocean virus capsids were highly enriched in negatively charged residues on internal and external surfaces. This adaptation likely helps maintain solubility at high salt concentrations and stabilizes ssDNA-capsid interactions by sequestering positively charged ions inside the capsid. At intersubunit interfaces, ocean capsids showed enrichment of cation-{pi} and {pi}-{pi} interactions, which are more resistant to solvation than salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Amino acid residues in lake capsids were more often substituted by biochemically dissimilar amino acids in ocean capsids than the reverse. Together, these results show that microvirus capsids adapt to high-salt environments through changes in surface charge and substitutions affecting intersubunit interactions. Further, we describe a general approach for studying the adaptation and stability of any protein family under complementary environmental or phenotypic conditions.

title: A proteomics screen of HIV-1 ASP interactors reveals multifaceted effects on host cell homeostasis
content: Nearly four decades after the identification of the HIV-1 antisense gene asp, the function of its protein product remains unclear. Evidence of ASP expression in vivo and the high degree of conservation of the asp gene among pandemic HIV-1 strains suggest a beneficial role for the virus. Using a mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics screen for ASP interactors, we identified nuclear, cytosolic, and mitochondrial host factors, congruent with variable sub-cellular ASP localization. A majority of the host factors identified in the MS screen are involved in pathways essential for host cell homeostasis, including DNA damage repair, intracellular protein transport, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Validating the biological relevance of these findings, we demonstrate that ASP shuttles to the nucleus to promote DNA damage repair and cell viability in response to genotoxic stress. We also finds that ASP promotes translation of mitochondrially encoded host proteins involved in cellular respiration and contributes to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential. Together, these studies identify ASP as a modulator of two major pathways of cellular homeostasis in infected cells, which has direct implications for HIV-1 persistence, spread, and the long-term survival of the viral reservoir.

title: Moderately acid-tolerant Nitrospira strains obtained by single-colony isolation on plates
content: Nitrospira are difficult to cultivate, and pure cultures are mainly obtained by dilution-to-extinction combined with other methods, a process that usually takes years to over a decade. Here, we isolated three Nitrospira strains from activated sludge and sediment within one year using conventional single-colony isolation. Pure cultures of two strains could grow and reform single colonies within 25-60 days on all three types of plates prepared with agar, agarose, and gellan gum. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed them within lineage I and indicated that they represent potential novel species, with the provisional names Nitrospira monocolonialis for strain Z02 and Nitrospira limosa for strains Z47 and Z70. All three strains were moderately acid-tolerant, with a minimum tolerable pH of 5.0; strain Z02 showed the highest acid tolerance, retaining 74% of its activity at pH 5.5. Strain Z02 was also highly adaptable to oxygen concentrations of 1-21%, retaining 78% and 85% of its maximum growth rate at 1% and 21% O2, respectively. Compared with the representative lineage I strain Nitrospira defluvii, all three strains contain superoxide dismutase encoding genes and some unique genes. Comparative transcriptomic analysis suggested that strain Z02 upregulated genes involved in stress responses, cell envelope modification, and putative type IVa pilus systems under acidic condition. Overall, this study provides the first demonstration that Nitrospira can grow on plates prepared with common gelling agents and form single colonies within a short period, and that Nitrospira can also tolerate moderately acid conditions.

title: Development of a core genome Multilocus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) and Life Identification Number (LIN) code schema for the Burkholderia cepacia complex
content: Background The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) currently comprises over 20 closely related species; however, understanding Bcc population biology is complicated due to the continual advances in taxonomy and diversity driven by extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Whilst there are conventional typing schemes for the Bcc, including Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), there remains a gap for fine-scale resolution typing of the species complex. Here, we present a 1,925 loci core genome MLST (cgMLST) and 14-digit Life Identification Number (LIN) barcoding scheme for the Bcc, that is embedded in the PubMLST database (https://PubMLST.org/organisms/burkholderia-cepacia-complex). Methods A dataset of 142 complete Bcc genomes spanning 19 species were downloaded from NCBI to develop the draft cgMLST scheme (Dataset 1). Two pangenome tools (PIRATE and PEPPAN) were then combined to give a consensus core gene list from Dataset 1. The 'core genes' from these outputs were then screened against the PubMLST loci, using a sequence tag scan, to identify their presence and curate new alleles. The core genes were then validated using a larger Bcc dataset (n = 934 genomes; 22 species) on PubMLST, which had been filtered for high-quality ([≤]200 contigs and 100% ribosomal MLST confidence). This refined the core gene list, ensuring a robust and reliable scheme using a threshold of 99% to classify the gene as 'core'. The population structure of the Bcc was subsequently analysed using the validation dataset to identify genetic clusters using ReporTree. Combined with statistical analysis, 14 allelic mismatch thresholds were identified for the LIN codes. Results The Bcc cgMLST scheme consists of 1,925 loci, which have been designated an arbitrary 'BCC' identifier. The cgMLST scheme and 14-threshold LIN code has been implemented in PubMLST and are publicly available for use. The Bcc genomes in the PubMLST database have been assigned cgSTs and LIN codes. Use cases of the LIN codes were validated using three previously published datasets, which spanned both outbreak investigation and phylogenomic lineage structures. Conclusions This stable, hierarchical LIN code nomenclature enhanced the ability to cluster isolates at multiple levels of resolution with examples overlayed on published datasets provided. The LIN code system is also backwards compatible with previous MLST and clonal complex (CC) nomenclature. Overall, the updated typing scheme will facilitate improve global public health through surveillance of the Bcc epidemiology including source tracing and outbreak investigation

title: Preclinical Development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a Human-Derived Swarming Strain, as a Live Biotherapeutic Product for Inflammatory Bowel Disease
content: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) remains an area of major unmet need, and the undefined composition and manufacturing burden of fecal microbiota transplantation have motivated a shift toward single-strain Live Biotherapeutic Products (LBPs). Swarming bacteria are enriched in the stressed gut and limit mucosal damage, but no human-derived swarming strain has been developed as an LBP. We therefore report the complete preclinical development of Enterobacter ludwigii LS57, a swarming strain isolated from human feces. Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) covered a three-tier cell bank, 30 L fed-batch fermentation and a colon-targeted enteric-coated capsule, enabling consistent pilot-scale production. No treatment-related findings emerged in safety pharmacology (Sprague-Dawley rats) or in single-dose and Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)-compliant 1-week repeat-dose toxicity studies (Sprague-Dawley rats and Beagle dogs). LS57 was identified as E. ludwigii by 16S rRNA and whole-genome sequencing and produced metabolites with reported anti-inflammatory activity in culture. In Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, LS57 reduced weight loss, preserved colon length, lowered colonic pro-inflammatory cytokines and remodeled the gut microbiota. It also attenuated Trinitrobenzene Sulfonic Acid (TNBS)-induced colitis and enhanced the effect of ciclosporin A. In vitro, LS57 was non-hemolytic, non-cytotoxic, and acid-labile, formed no biofilm, and its resistance to aminopenicillins, cephamycins and imipenem was not transferable by conjugation. In vivo, LS57 colonized the inflamed colon without translocation in wild-type and interleukin-10-deficient mice, and experimental bacteremia was treatable with gentamicin or levofloxacin. LS57 combines efficacy across two mechanistically distinct colitis models with a safety package that addresses the principal regulatory concerns for LBPs, and a scalable manufacturing process, compatible with current good manufacturing practice, in which enteric coating overcomes the strain's poor gastric survival. These data support clinical development of LS57 in IBD.

title: Effect of Lactobacillus postbiotic supplementation on intestinal permeability, nutrient digestibility, and gut microbial and metabolic profiles in aging cats
content: Aging in cats is associated with declining nutrient digestibility and increased intestinal permeability, but evidence supporting microbiome-targeted interventions in older cats remains limited. We investigated whether daily supplementation with the Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic LB fermentate HF (LBHF) affected intestinal permeability, apparent total tract digestibility, gut microbiome composition, and fecal and plasma metabolomic profiles in older cats. Twenty cats aged 7.7-13.8 years were enrolled in a blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial comprising two 29-day treatment periods separated by a 28-day washout; 18 cats completed both periods. Intestinal permeability was the primary endpoint, while nutrient digestibility, microbiome composition, and metabolomic profiles were secondary endpoints. LBHF did not affect intestinal permeability or absorptive capacity relative to placebo, although intestinal permeability was positively associated with age. Overall nutrient digestibility was higher during LBHF treatment, with the clearest endpoint-specific evidence observed for protein digestibility. LBHF was associated with a non-significant overall increase in Shannon diversity and a reduction in the relative abundance of Streptococcus lutetiensis. The increase in Shannon diversity was significant only in cats receiving placebo followed by LBHF, indicating a treatment-sequence-dependent response. Thirty-three plasma and 29 fecal metabolites showed significantly different changes during LBHF treatment compared with placebo. Plasma metabolites generally showed more positive changes during LBHF treatment, whereas most associated fecal metabolites showed more negative changes. Sequence-stratified microbiome and metabolome responses differed substantially, suggesting possible period, treatment-order, or carryover effects. Overall, LBHF did not improve intestinal permeability but was well tolerated and improved nutrient digestibility, particularly protein digestibility, while producing modest and sequence-dependent microbiome and metabolome responses. These findings suggest that the effects of LBHF in healthy older cats may relate more strongly to digestive efficiency and host metabolic responses than to intestinal permeability.

title: Multiple adaptive trajectories shape antimalarial resistance evolution in Ethiopian Plasmodium falciparum
content: Plasmodium falciparum malaria continues to impose a substantial public health burden across sub-Saharan Africa, with Ethiopia experiencing a recent resurgence in malaria cases. We analysed whole genome data from 120 P. falciparum isolates collected in 2024 across five ecologically and epidemiologically diverse transmission settings in Ethiopia and placed these in the context of 1,220 publicly available genomes. Parasite populations were highly structured within Ethiopia, while Horn of Africa isolates formed a genetically distinct regional cluster relative to East and West African populations. We identified evidence of recent positive selection surrounding the artemisinin resistance associated PfK13 R622I variant and detected co-occurrence with Pfcrt mutations together with recurrent selection signals at genes within the PfK13-associated haemoglobin endocytosis pathway, including Pfmca2, Pfkic7, Pfkic8 and Pfkic9. We further observed the emergence of the PfPX1 D384A-PIN haplotype, with shared identity-by-descent linking Ethiopian and Ugandan carriers, supporting a recent introduction followed by local selection. Widespread Pfhrp2/3 deletions occurred on diverse genetic backgrounds. Together, these findings reveal a complex adaptive landscape shaped by antimalarial and diagnostic selection pressures and suggest that parasite evolution in the Horn of Africa proceeds through multiple adaptive trajectories, rather than through the spread of a single dominant lineage.

title: Women's health outreach using a rapid and fieldable Nanopore-based microbiome profiling workflow.
content: Background In recent years, scientific interest in the vaginal microbiome has increased due to its impact on women's health. Colonization of the Lactobacillus species in the vagina may contribute to protection against vaginal infectious diseases. In order to create public awareness regarding vaginal health and to provide insights into the vaginal microbiome, a rapid field microbiome analysis using Nanopore sequencing was evaluated at Lowlands, a three-day music festival in the Netherlands. This study aimed not only to evaluate a rapid sequencing workflow, but also to explore citizen science as a tool for health promotion and public engagement in women's health. Methods The workflow at Lowlands contained the following steps; (i) Dialogue concerning vaginal health, with invitation to participate. (ii) Informed consent and questionnaire to investigate knowledge on vaginal health, life-style and contraceptive usage; (iii) self-collection of a vaginal swab; (iv) DNA isolation using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution; (v) Ultrafast amplification of the 16S rRNA gene using NextGenPCR thermal cycling using 16S Barcoding kit 24 V14; (vi) Library preparation and sequencing was performed according to the manufacturers protocol using R10 chemistry; (vii) For data-analysis, MABA16S was used, with slight modifications. This workflow was established within 4 hours and results were communicated with interested participants.

title: Northern palsa and peat ecosystem microbiomes are potentially supported by hydrogen and carbon monoxide metabolism
content: Northern peatland and permafrost ecosystems are facing rapid changes, with increasing temperatures, permafrost thaw and shifts in hydrology. Characterizing microbial communities and metabolic potential from the soils and associated water bodies is crucial to understanding the changes in biogeochemical cycling in these ecosystems. For this, samples were collected and sequenced from subarctic palsa and peat soils, along with samples from associated thaw ponds and streams. Metagenomics was utilized in describing the microbiome and its metabolic potential in these environments. Palsa soils hosted microbial communities that were distinct from the peatland soils, ponds and stream waters. Soils and their adjacent ponds shared taxa, and peat soils and ponds also shared taxa with the streams, unlike palsa soils which were likely more hydrologically isolated. Based on metabolic marker gene ratio for denitrification [(nirS+nirK)/nosZ], palsa soils had the strongest potential to be a source of nitrous oxide (N2O) out of all the sample types. Marker genes for hydrogen gas (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) utilization were abundant across soil environments and metagenome assembled genomes, suggesting that trace gas oxidation is likely one of the key energy sources for microbiomes. In the palsa ponds and peat soils pmoA, marker gene for methanotrophy, was the most abundant compared to the other sample types.

title: Gene-resolved metagenomics reveals partitioned nitrogen transformation potential in a landfill leachate sequencing batch reactor microbiome
content: Landfill leachate can contain high concentrations of ammonia and organic nitrogen requiring treatment before discharge. Sequencing batch reactors (SBRs) promote biological nitrogen removal through alternating aerobic and anoxic conditions, but taxonomic profiling alone cannot resolve how nitrogen transformation and competing retention pathways are distributed across microbial communities. This study applied gene-resolved metagenomics to a sludge sample collected from a UK landfill leachate SBR. Nitrogen-metabolism genes were linked to contig-level taxonomic assignments and metagenome-assembled genome bins to examine nitrification, denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), and assimilatory nitrate reduction (ANR). Nitrogen-transformation potential was partitioned across dominant and minor taxa. Nitrospirota and Pseudomonadota were the most abundant classified phyla, whereas Actinomycetota represented only 4% of the community but included Actinomycetes, which showed the highest within-taxon proportion of nitrogen metabolism associated genes. amoABC was assigned only to Nitrosomonas and Nitrososphaerota, whereas denitrification genes were more widely distributed but frequently occurred as partial pathways. nosZ was detected only in the minor phyla Chloroflexota, Acidobacteriota and Myxococcota. DNRA and ANR-associated genes occurred across multiple lineages; nirA in Nitrospira and DNRA-associated nirBD elsewhere within Nitrospirota suggested nitrifier-associated lineages may also encode nitrogen retention potential. Gene-resolved metagenomics identified candidate low-abundance contributors, restricted distributions of genes associated with ammonia oxidation and nitrous oxide reduction, and nitrogen-retention potential not apparent from taxonomic composition alone. Because the study examined DNA-level potential in a single sludge sample, expression, reactor chemistry and longitudinal data are needed to establish pathway activity and operational relevance.

title: Functional Conservation Amid Extreme Divergence in Freshwater SAR11 Hypervariable Region 2
content: The Ca. Pelagibacterales order (SAR11) is a ubiquitous bacterioplankton in aquatic ecosystems. The genomes of SAR11 bacteria contain hypervariable region 2 (HVR2), the largest HVR with extreme diversity. Previous studies collectively indicated the enrichment of cell-surface modification genes on HVR2, which have been hypothesized to facilitate phage evasion. However, characterisation of HVR2 has primarily targeted marine clades and been limited for freshwater SAR11 (aka. Fontibacterium). Here, we employed single-cell genomics and recovered 176 Fontibacterium HVR2 sequences from Lake Biwa (Japan) and Lake Zurich (Switzerland), across multiple sampling years for Lake Biwa. Comparative sequence analyses revealed that freshwater HVR2 showed high intra-population diversity and appears to evolve independently of the rest of the genome, mirroring patterns observed in marine counterparts. Nevertheless, highly conserved HVR2 sequence pairs were observed for distinct Fontibacterium species from the two intercontinental habitats, suggesting horizontal transfers of HVR2 with conserved functional configurations across divergent lineages and large spatial scales. Further comparison with 145 marine HVR2 sequences revealed HVR2 sequences displaying synteny between Fontibacterium and marine SAR11, and 209 gene families conserved across habitats, including three near-universally conserved families. All examined freshwater HVR2s contained initiator methionine tRNA genes concentrated near the boundaries of the 5S region, suggesting a tDNA-anchored integration mechanism. These results suggest the functional equivalence of HVR2 across marine and freshwater SAR11 clades, and the existence of a shared pool of HVR2 sequences that evolve reticulately through mutual genetic exchange, independent of the vertical inheritance of the rest of the genome.

title: Ecological opportunity and evolutionary relatedness predict parasite sharing differently across mammalian taxonomic scales
content: As global change brings species into new contact, understanding the ecological and evolutionary drivers of parasite sharing is essential for anticipating and mitigating disease emergence. Yet, the relative importance of geographic proximity and evolutionary relatedness among host species in predicting parasite sharing remains unresolved. We tested whether their relative importance changes across host taxonomic scale using 30,310 recorded associations between 680 mammalian and 11,107 parasite species. Geography accounted for 86.6% importance within genera, declining to 44.7% across all mammals, shifting toward evolutionary relatedness predominating. Parasite sharing increased nonlinearly with geographic proximity and host relatedness, and the overall trend varied among parasite types. Notably, accounting for host taxonomic scale improved parasite-sharing prediction accuracy. To explore the consequences of biotic homogenization, we applied a counterfactual scenario of reducing geographic distance by 99%, which increased mean predicted parasite sharing to 13.71% within genera and 1.50% at the class level. Together, these findings suggest that ecological opportunity is especially consequential among close relatives whereas evolutionary similarity is increasingly important among geographically distant species. Accounting for evolutionary scale can therefore improve sharing predictions and help identify which new host encounters warrant surveillance for cross-species transmission and disease emergence.

title: US water protection maps undercount wetlands | Science
content: On 9 September 2026, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) proposed narrowing the definition of “waters of the United States,” limiting federal wetland protection to those touching perennial water. This criterion reduces eligible wetlands even further than the 2023 Sackett v. EPA standard did (1, 2). After the Sackett decision, 19 to 91% of nontidal wetlands were at risk of losing protection, depending on interpretation (3). The EPA’s own regulatory analysis could not produce a reliable national estimate and relied on qualitative judgment instead (4), in part because its National Wetlands Inventory (NWI), which was partially built from decades-old aerial photography, was not designed for regulatory use (4). Obtaining more-accurate and up-to-date wetland maps is therefore essential before revisiting the US rules that define protected waters.

title: Immobilized Epiphytic Bacteria Enhance Macrophyte Suppression of a Bloom‐Forming Cyanobacterium
content:
First isolation of algicidal epiphytic Priestia megaterium BW from submerged macrophytes; it kills Microcystis aeruginosa via metabolic disruption, oxidative stress and cell collapse. Confirms high efficacy of Vallisneria natans + immobilized BW for synergistic algal control.

ABSTRACT
Harmful cyanobacterial blooms are an increasing threat to freshwater ecosystems and water security worldwide. Biological control using macrophytes or algicidal bacteria is often studied separately despite natural co‐occurrence. Here we show that the epiphytic bacterium Priestia megaterium strain BW, isolated from submerged macrophytes, exhibits strong algicidal activity and forms an enhanced suppression system with its host plant Vallisneria natans. Pre‐colonization of BW on V. natans leaves achieves > 80% inhibition of Microcystis aeruginosa biomass within 5 days. When immobilized on a ceramic material carrier, BW rapidly suppresses algal photosynthetic efficiency within 48 h. Mechanistically, the algicidal effect follows a multi‐pathway process involving early photosynthetic impairment, oxidative stress and subsequent cellular disintegration. Notably, the combined application of immobilized BW with V. natans produces stronger and faster suppression than either the bacterium or the plant alone. Our findings demonstrate that an epiphytic bacterium can retain potent algicidal activity outside its native biofilm and that its efficacy is markedly enhanced when re‐integrated with the plant, providing direct evidence for plant–microbe synergistic control of cyanobacterial blooms.

title: Endophytic Success of Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli in Plants via Root Uptake Is Governed by Stochasticity in Transpiration
content:
Foodborne pathogens like Salmonella and E. coli can stochastically internalize through plant roots and colonize plant leaves, where equally exposed plants may harbour dangerously high levels of microbes or remain uncontaminated. The internalization stochasticity is influenced by temperature and plant transpiration, posing challenges in traditional mitigation strategies in agriculture.

ABSTRACT
Human foodborne pathogens can internalize into edible plant tissues through root uptake, yet the mechanisms governing this process remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a localized enrichment inoculation system that enables robust and reproducible investigation of bacterial internalization in plants. Using Arabidopsis thaliana and multiple microgreen species, we show that Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli rapidly penetrate intact roots and translocate to shoots independent of bacterial motility, virulence, plant immunity or root tissue damage. Instead, internalization is strongly associated with plant transpiration activity. Transcriptomic and physiological analyses revealed that stochastic variation in photosynthesis and transpiration between genetically identical plants underlies highly heterogeneous contamination outcomes, producing near‐bimodal distributions of bacterial load among individual plants. Suppression of transpiration through cooling or abscisic acid treatment significantly reduced pathogen internalization. These findings establish plant physiological stochasticity as a critical determinant of foodborne pathogen uptake and reveal new opportunities for mitigation strategies in agriculture.

When these stressors occur together it results in compound events. We used advanced computer models to project how compound events will evolve around Hawaii during the 21st century. title: Simulated In‐Stream CO2 Production Under Changing Organic Carbon Quantity, Quality, and Stream Geochemistry
content:
Abstract
Increasing urbanization and changing precipitation confound our understanding of carbon (C) cycling in streams. Precipitation drives organic C into waterways, while watershed urbanization can increase the lability of dissolved organic carbon (DOC). Uncertainty in how C quantity and quality interact to influence in‐stream CO2 production limits predictions of stream responses to urbanization and extreme precipitation. To investigate these effects, we simulated in‐stream CO2 production and aqueous CO2 dynamics across Baltimore watersheds (Maryland, USA) spanning an urbanization gradient using a multi‐pool stream carbon decomposition model. The model couples microbial CO2 production with carbonate speciation of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) to estimate aqueous CO2. We hypothesized that precipitation‐driven C loading and urbanization‐enhanced DOC lability would increase in‐stream CO2 production more in urban than in exurban streams. Scenario‐based simulations were designed to evaluate this hypothesis under a range of precipitation and urbanization conditions. Our model suggests that C loading generally has a larger effect on in‐stream CO2 production than DOC lability alone, with the greatest CO2 production occurring when both C loading and lability increase simultaneously. However, response magnitude depended on initial stream geochemistry. At the most urbanized, DIC‐rich site, precipitation‐driven dilution reduced the carbonate‐derived contribution to aqueous CO2, outweighing increases in microbial CO2 production even when DOC lability increased simultaneously. These results suggest that aqueous in‐stream CO2 is governed by C quantity, quality, and initial stream geochemistry, highlighting the importance of considering interactions among precipitation, land use, and stream geochemistry when evaluating C processing in rivers.

title: Flow‐Dependent Phosphate Oxygen Isotope (δ18O‐PO43−) Signatures in Tile Drainage From Two Long‐Term Tillage Systems
content:
Abstract
Dissolved phosphorus exported through tile drainage is quantified by concentration, which integrates multiple pools and pathways but cannot indicate how it was processed or mobilized. Whether its isotopic composition varies with hydrologic state and management is unknown. We monitored two adjacent fields at the R.J. Cook Agronomy Farm Long‐Term Agroecosystem Research site, under conventional tillage (CT) and no‐till (NT) since 1998, combining 15‐min discharge records (104,577 observations), dual water isotopes, and phosphate oxygen isotopes (δ18O‐PO43−; n = 54 on 27 paired dates). Dissolved reactive phosphorus was higher in the NT field (0.074 vs. 0.047 mg P L−1) under both baseflow and event flow, but area‐normalized export was similar (0.066 and 0.072 kg ha−1) because the CT field drained more water per hectare. In contrast, δ18O‐PO43− showed a crossing response, declining with discharge in the CT field (13.9–12.3‰) and rising in the NT field (12.5–15.0‰). The system‐by‐flow interaction (4.09‰; 95% CI 2.54–5.64) persisted across shared‐threshold, continuous‐discharge, percentile‐rank, date‐blocked, and leave‐one‐out analyses. Deviations from a per‐sample tile‐water reference were used only as a standardized comparison value. With one field per system, these patterns do not demonstrate a causal effect of tillage. They do yield a testable hypothesis: that NT event flow delivers phosphate through preferential pathways from near‐surface pools with limited oxygen exchange, whereas CT event flow mobilizes phosphate processed within the soil matrix. Testing it requires flow‐stratified δ18O‐PO43− sampling, measured soil‐P end members, and depth‐resolved water isotopes at replicated sites.

title: Diel and Seasonal Variation in Surface‐Water CO2 Partial Pressure in an Agricultural Reservoir in Japan
content:
Abstract
As sources of carbon dioxide (CO2), the most important greenhouse gas, lakes and reservoirs influence the global carbon cycle. Although CO2 partial pressure (pCO2) in inland waters exhibits marked diel variation, its seasonal trends and controlling factors remain unclear. Based on measurements conducted at 30‐min intervals on >170 days over a 1‐year period, we demonstrated the general pattern of diel variations in pCO2 in the surface water of a shallow agricultural reservoir in Japan and revealed that these variations changed seasonally. Daily maximum and minimum pCO2 levels occurred in the early morning and afternoon, respectively, throughout the year, but were reached earlier in summer and later in winter. The diel range of pCO2 values was 336–6,729 μatm, with higher and lower values in summer and winter, respectively. Ignoring this diel variation could lead to an error range of −40% to +60% for annual average pCO2 estimates, causing over‐ or underestimation of CO2 emissions from shallow inland waters. However, we found that this error could be kept within ±5% by taking ≤6‐hr measurements. Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) and/or water temperature (Tw) were the main drivers of diel pCO2 variation, reflecting their roles in regulating photosynthesis and respiration. The magnitude and direction of the effects of Tw on pCO2 also varied seasonally. It is anticipated that frequent monitoring of pCO2, PAR, and Tw will improve our understanding of CO2 dynamics in shallow inland water bodies.

title: Impact of Winter Convection on Carbon Variability in the South Adriatic Gyre: A 1D Argo‐Driven Modeling Approach
content:
Abstract
Understanding the variability of air–sea carbon dioxide (CO2) fluxes is fundamental for quantifying the ocean's role in the global carbon cycle. While large‐scale and long‐term flux patterns are relatively well constrained, the processes driving variability at regional and shorter temporal scales remain poorly understood. Addressing this gap is crucial for improving our understanding of how physical and biogeochemical processes modulate ocean‐atmospheric carbon exchange. In this study, we used a one‐dimensional Argo‐driven model to assess the air–sea CO2 flux in the persistent gyre of the South Adriatic Sea (SAd Sea). The General Ocean Turbulence Model was coupled with the Biogeochemical Flux Model through the Framework for Aquatic Biogeochemical Models, and constrained by quality‐controlled Argo observations of temperature and salinity. Model outputs were validated against Biogeochemical Argo measurements and partial pressure of CO2 (pCO2) observations collected at the EMSO‐E2M3A South Adriatic Observatory (EMSO‐E2M3A). Tuning the initial carbonate‐system conditions highlighted the importance of accurately representing deep‐water dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and total alkalinity distributions for simulating winter pCO2 variability. The SAd Sea acted as a weak sink of atmospheric CO2 (0.99 $0.99$ mmolCm−2d−1 $\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{o}\mathrm{l}\mathrm{C}{\mathrm{m}}^{-2}{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}$), with strong seasonal variability driven by temperature‐controlled solubility and pronounced daily variability imposed by wind forcing. Consistent with EMSO‐E2M3A observations, our model reproduced annually recurrent secondary pCO2 peaks, which reduced the air–sea pCO2 gradient and, consequently, the ocean CO2 uptake. Sensitivity experiments revealed that these peaks resulted from the upwelling of DIC‐rich waters induced by wind‐driven mixing and deep convection processes.

title: Satellite Observations of Annual Variations in the Ocean‐Induced Magnetic Field From the Tropical Oceans
content:
Abstract
The Ocean Induced Magnetic Field (OIMF) is produced by the motion of the electrically conducting ocean through Earth's ambient magnetic field, and its time‐dependence carries information concerning ocean dynamics and electrical conductivity changes. Here, we present an algorithm to estimate, from satellite magnetic field observations, the band‐limited OIMF, focusing on annual variations (periods 300–430 days) and spherical harmonic degrees 19 to 28. We work with Along‐Track and East‐West differences of the vector magnetic field and intensity measured by the Swarm satellite constellation. After applying corrections for known non‐oceanic signals, we construct a time‐dependent internal field model which is subsequently filtered in space and time to provide an estimate of the OIMF. We assess this estimate via comparisons to a simulated OIMF computed from the Copernicus CMEMS mean ocean model that is based on assimilated oceanographic observations. Focusing on the tropics during the solar minimum years 2018.5–2020.5, we find modest but encouraging localized agreement between the estimated and simulated OIMF in the Indian Ocean (correlation coefficient of 0.3 for spatial structures, up to 0.8 in time‐longitude plots). The agreement is in terms of spatial‐temporal structures rather than amplitude. In other ocean basins, where the OIMF in the studied spatio‐temporal band is weaker, we find less agreement, with the exception of some parts of the central Pacific and the western North Atlantic. Our results suggest it is possible to retrieve the general circulation OIMF from satellite magnetic field measurements, in regions where the ocean‐induced signal is strong, provided sufficient, high quality, geomagnetically‐quiet, satellite data are available.

title: Climate‐Modulated Sediment Transport Processes in Decadal Shoreline Evolution Across Contrasting Coasts
content:
Abstract
Coastal shoreline evolution results from sediment transport processes governed by wave conditions and water‐level variability, both of which are modulated by large‐scale climate forcing across multiple timescales. While equilibrium shoreline models often reproduce short‐term shoreline fluctuations, they are less able to reproduce interannual or decadal variability, particularly where climate‐driven modulation of sediment transport is important. Here, we investigate how wave, water‐level, and large‐scale climate variability jointly control shoreline behavior over multi‐decadal periods using a reduced‐complexity shoreline evolution framework. We analyze three contrasting coastal environments: a high‐wave‐energy, microtidal embayed beach (Narrabeen‐Collaroy Beach, Australia); a low‐to‐medium‐wave‐energy, microtidal sandy barrier island (Madeira Beach, Florida); and a moderate‐to‐high‐wave‐energy lake shoreline characterized by significant water‐level variability (Ontonagon, Michigan). Together, these sites represent a broad range of coastal settings. Short‐term shoreline fluctuations are separated from long‐term trends, and shoreline evolution is evaluated using blind forecasts exceeding 10 years. Results show that climate forcing exerts a persistent influence on sediment transport and long‐term shoreline trajectories that cannot be explained by wave forcing alone. The findings indicate that the long‐term evolution of shorelines is shaped by the cumulative effects of wave dynamics, water levels, and climate forcing. Recognizing this influence is essential for understanding shoreline evolution under climate variability and for improving projections of long‐term coastal change.

title: Waterworld: increasing coastal urban waterways and the dilemmas for ecology and society
content: Coastal urban expansion has transformed shorelines worldwide, replacing wetlands and floodplains with engineered residential waterways. The rapid proliferation of artificial canals and islands, from Palm Islands in the United Arab Emirates to China's coastal megaprojects, has created a global form of “ocean sprawl”, yet its ecological consequences remain largely unquantified. Here, by analyzing Google Earth satellite imagery, we recorded 4389 km of urban waterways, a 10.3% expansion of such waterways since our 2007 assessment, and evaluated the extent to which these systems have been studied for ecological, hydrological, and environmental impacts. Despite over 50 years of construction, empirical evidence remains sparse, and sustainability interventions are rarely tested. Our findings highlight the urgent need for systematic evaluation frameworks that guide both the design of new waterways and in retrofitting existing developments. Such approaches are essential to ensure that expanding ocean sprawl delivers measurable benefits for biodiversity, the environment, and local communities.

title: Decomposition of the S. aureus pangenome reveals evolving genetic repertoire associated with adaptation and virulence
content:
by Siddharth M. Chauhan, Bernhard O. Palsson, Jonathan M. Monk

Bacterial pangenomes are mosaics of vertically inherited chromosomal backgrounds and horizontally acquired mobile elements, yet existing analysis methods either assign each genome to a single phylogenetic group or treat genes independently, failing to resolve this composite architecture. Here, we show that non-negative matrix factorization decomposes the accessory pangenome of 1,398 curated Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules (“phylons”) that cleanly separate lineage-defining components from mobile genetic element repertoires, achieving 90% reconstruction accuracy with 96% precision. The additive representation, where each genome equals a primary lineage phylon plus one or more mobilome phylons, recovers known biology (clonal complex structure, immune evasion cluster types) and reveals previously uncharacterized structure, including multiple horizontal transfer events linking the CC30 and hybrid ST239 pandemic lineages. Annotation-independent validation with geNomad confirmed that 75–96% of mobilome phylon gene instances physically reside within prophage regions across all 1,398 genomes, while coordinate-level analysis of the remainder revealed prophage boundary effects, chromosomally integrated elements, and composite mobilome architecture rather than false assignments. External validation on 966 independent draft genome assemblies yielded zero false-positive lineage assignments (mean AUC = 0.996) with no dependence on assembly quality, and mobilome phylons discriminated human from livestock hosts and methicillin-resistant from methicillin-susceptible isolates without retraining. A lightweight projection tool, phylon_assign, enables rapid classification of new genomes. The generalization of this framework from Escherichia coli and Enterobacter to Staphylococcus aureus – species with fundamentally different pangenome structures – establishes non-negative matrix factorization as a scalable, organism-agnostic approach for resolving the modular architecture of bacterial pangenomes.

title: The importance of genes does not predict their mutation rate
content:
by Sofia Radrizzani, Laurence D. Hurst

The convention that mutation is a random process has been challenged by suggestions that selection has acted on between-gene variation in the mutation rate, with claims that more important genes are protected from mutation in part, in prokaryotes, by being on the leading strand, while those required for rapid adaptive evolution have higher mutation rates, in part by being on the lagging strand. The original selectionist claims have proven contentious with several replication failures. However, none of the replication attempts fully allow for covariates and many employ data from mismatch repair (MMR) knockout strains. To address these limitations, we consider amassed mutation accumulation data for wild-type Escherichia coli, the focal species for adaptive claims, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, in a multiple parameter-controlled analysis to predict between-gene variation in mutational density (mutations per base pair). Along with covariates, we consider putative selectively relevant parameters: protein level and essentiality to capture genic “importance”, and, in E. coli, strand with respect to DNA replication. We consider deviation of correlation and partial correlation values from those expected under trinucleotide-controlled simulations. While in E. coli more highly transcribed genes may have slightly lower mutation rates, potentially consistent with a selectionist model, the same is not seen in yeast, and in neither species do genes for more abundant or essential proteins have lower mutation rates. In E. coli there is no difference in mutation rate between genes on different strands, a lack of difference replicated in other prokaryotes. The degree of purifying selection is also not predictive of mutation density. We additionally highlight a strong artefact seen using the standard off-the-shelf statistical approach and note that results from MMR-deficient strains are discordant. We conclude that as trends are nearly uniformly unsupportive, not consistent between species and of miniscule effect size, they present no challenge to convention.

title: Neural integration of acoustic statistics enables mice to detect acoustic targets in noise
content:
by Artoghrul Alishbayli, Karol Przewrocki, Paul van Heumen, Bernhard Englitz

Sound detection amidst noise presents an important challenge in audition. Many naturally occurring sounds (rain, wind) can be described and predicted only statistically, so-called sound textures. Previous research has demonstrated the human ability to leverage this statistical predictability for sound recognition, but the neural mechanisms remain elusive. We trained mice to detect vocalizations embedded in sound textures with different statistical predictability, while recording and optogenetically modulating the neural activity in the auditory cortex. Mice showed improved performance and neural encoding if they could sample the statistics longer per trial. Textures with more exploitable structure, specifically higher cross-frequency correlations improved behavioral performance as well as neural representation of vocalizations. Activating parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons had an asymmetric effect depending on the acoustic context, improving detection and neural encoding of vocalizations for low correlations, and impoverishing them for high cross-frequency correlations. In summary, mice exploit stimulus statistics to improve sound detection in naturalistic background noise, reflected in behavioral performance and neural activity, relying on PV interneurons for temporal integration.

title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information
content:
by Sahil Luthra, Raha N. Razin, Adam T. Tierney, Lori L. Holt, Frederic Dick

Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of ‘alien identity’ and two classes of ‘alien size.’ Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

title: Life-cycle plasticity enables conditional asexual reproduction in a kelp
content:
by Daniel Liesner, Rémy Luthringer, Lineekela Kandjengo, John J. Bolton, Mark D. Rothman, Myriam Valero, Fabian B. Haas, Susana M. Coelho

Many organisms alternate between distinct life stages and can reproduce either sexually or asexually, yet the mechanisms coordinating these developmental and reproductive transitions remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the molecular basis of life stage identity and reproductive mode in the kelp Laminaria pallida, a multicellular organism with a complex life cycle. By combining gene expression analyses with developmental experiments and natural population-level approaches, we characterize the transcriptional signatures associated with developmental state transitions in both sexual and asexual contexts. We show that asexual reproduction is associated with endoreduplication and reduced fitness, while it is retained but rarely expressed in two natural populations. Moreover, we find that the presence of potential mating partners reduces asexual development, revealing that reproductive mode is adjusted in response to reproductive opportunities. Together, these findings suggest that asexual reproduction functions as a conditional alternative to sex, promoting persistence when sexual reproduction is constrained while preserving the long-term benefits of sexual reproduction when mates are available. More broadly, our results reveal how organisms integrate developmental, environmental, and reproductive cues to balance alternative reproductive strategies across complex life cycles.

title: Nitrogen uptake regimes in the Weddell-Scotia Confluence during late austral summer: The key role of ammonium

Author(s): Flavio Emiliano Paparazzo

title: Learning-associated flexibility of cortical taste coding is impaired in Shank3 knockout mice
content: The ability to update the valence of sensory perception to influence behavior is crucial for survival. A common phenotype in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) is defects in sensory processing, but whether these defects impair flexible sensory encoding is largely unexplored. In particular, how genetic risk factors such as Shank3 deletion affect the adaptability of cortical taste processing and downstream behavior is unknown. To address this gap, we performed two-photon calcium imaging during a conditioned taste aversion (CTA) learning paradigm, an ethologically relevant form of associative learning that depends on taste processing in the gustatory cortex (GC), to examine how Shank3 knockout alters taste-related neuronal activity in GC and influences CTA learning. We found that GC neurons in Shank3 knockout mice exhibited reduced stimulus-evoked suppression and increased trial-to-trial correlated variability during the acquisition of CTA memory. These activity changes, which likely reduced signal-to-noise ratio in GC, were associated with slower CTA acquisition in Shank3 knockout mice. In both genotypes, CTA learning enhanced, while subsequent extinction reduced, taste discriminability in GC, and both extinction and the associated reduction in discriminability were faster in Shank3 knockout than in wild-type mice. Together, these results show that Shank3 loss is associated with destabilized cortical activity dynamics in GC, which may contribute to inefficient encoding and maintenance of learned taste aversion. These findings show that loss of Shank3 compromises the ability of animals to update behavior to incorporate negative outcomes, and suggest this loss of flexibility may be an important feature of monogenic ASDs.

title: Synthetic torpor in the rat protects the heart from ischaemia-reperfusion injury
content: During times of environmental stress, many animals enter torpor: a reversible protective physiological state typically characterised by reductions in core temperature, heart rate, and oxygen consumption. Species that naturally enter this hypothermic and hypometabolic state are tolerant of ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Consequently, there is a growing interest in utilising aspects of torpor for clinical applications such as protection from stroke or myocardial infarction. It is currently unknown, however, whether a torpor-like state is protective in animals that do not naturally enter torpor. Using viral vector-mediated chemogenetic activation of the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, we induced synthetic torpor in the rat, a species that does not naturally enter torpor. We demonstrate this state is cardioprotective in an ex vivo ischaemia-reperfusion injury model with an ~40% reduction in infarct size. Synthetic torpor-induced cardioprotection of the normothermic, isolated heart is not dependent on prior hypothermia in vivo. Phosphoproteomic analysis of cardiac tissue indicates that the protective effects of synthetic torpor may be mediated by parallel activation of cell survival and stress tolerance pathways and inhibition of cell death pathways. These findings provide important insights into the mechanisms of organ protective effects of synthetic torpor states with implications for future clinical translation in humans.

title: Sustained Ice Loss and Ice‐Shelf Flow Reorganization in the Carney‐Duncan Sector, Marie Byrd Land, West Antarctica (2010–2026)
content:
Abstract
Small islands and ice rumples can regulate ice‐shelf flow, but conventional satellite altimetry poorly resolves their evolution. Here we use CryoSat‐2 SARIn swath altimetry to quantify surface‐elevation and volume changes over the Carney‐Duncan sector at the outer margin of West Antarctica's Getz Ice Shelf. From July 2010 to March 2026, this sector lost ice at a rate of approximately 2.1 km3 yr−1, resulting in an integrated loss of more than 30 km3. Thinning was concentrated along valley troughs and fast‐flowing corridors, where swath‐derived estimates resolve stronger thinning than the previous multi‐mission altimetry product. Landsat imagery shows progressive unanchoring of the ice rumple within the Carney‐Duncan passage since 1973, with more pronounced retreat after 2002, accompanied by local speed‐up and flow reorganization linked to the Stockholm and Bali Glaciers. These results link localized thinning to weakened pinning and demonstrate that changes in small peripheral features can reorganize Antarctic ice‐shelf flow.

title: Data‐Driven Parameterization of Arctic Ocean Turbulent Mixing
content:
Abstract
Turbulent mixing may become increasingly important in a changing Arctic Ocean, influencing regional dynamics and global overturning. Arctic turbulence remains poorly characterized due to sparse observations, limitations of conventional parameterizations, and incomplete understanding. We train gradient‐boosted decision trees on global microstructure turbulence data (>5,000 profiles; ∼3×105 $3\times 1{0}^{5}$ data points) to predict turbulent dissipation from more widely available hydrography. Global training is essential for skill across non‐Arctic and Arctic regions (R2=0.75 ${R}^{2}=0.75$, 75% within a factor of 2 of observations; R2 ${R}^{2}$ = 0.47–0.55 under spatial block cross‐validation). Applied to pan‐Arctic hydrographic observations, predictions show enhanced dissipation along margins and shelves and weaker values in basin interiors, consistent with current understanding. Applied to high‐resolution model output, predictions reveal diffusivities and a basin‐integrated irreversible buoyancy flux consistent with observations, yet markedly different from the common K‐Profile Parameterization—with implications for simulated tracer transport. Our parameterization can help assess climate‐mixing feedbacks in projections while physics‐based parameterizations mature.

title: Long‐Term Strengthening of the Summer Indian Ocean Subtropical Cell and Its Underlying Mechanisms
content:
Abstract
The Indian Ocean Subtropical Cell (STC) is a shallow overturning circulation that links the subtropical and equatorial oceans and plays a key role in redistributing heat. Although strongest during boreal summer, its long‐term evolution remains poorly understood. Using multiple ocean reanalysis and pacemaker experiments, we show that the summer STC has significantly strengthened since 1980 (−0.047 ± 0.010 Sv yr−1). The experiments identify enhanced subtropical easterlies over the southern Indian Ocean, driven by the non‐uniform warming of the Indo‐Pacific warm pool, as an important contributor. The strengthened easterlies reinforce the STC by enhancing surface Ekman transport, promoting the subduction of subtropical waters into the thermocline, and strengthening subsurface geostrophic transport. These findings reveal how Indo‐Pacific warm‐pool warming reshapes tropical overturning circulation and improves our understanding of the oceanic response to global warming.

title: Greenland and Antarctica Dominate Recent Acceleration in Global Mean Sea Level Rise: 1993–2023
content:
Abstract
Global mean sea level (GMSL) rise has accelerated over the last three decades, with satellite altimetry indicating an acceleration of 0.07 ± 0.03 mm/yr2 over 1993–2023. However, the specific contributions of Greenland and Antarctica to this acceleration budget have remained insufficiently quantified. We extend satellite gravimetry estimates of Greenland and Antarctica ice mass changes back to 1993, enabling a comprehensive 31‐year assessment of their contributions to GMSL acceleration and providing an independent record for cross‐validation with other observational and modeling data sets. Ice mass loss has accelerated by −8.5 ± 4.0 Gt/yr2 for Greenland and −4.6 ± 1.3 Gt/yr2 for Antarctica from 1993 to 2023. These results are consistent across multiple data sets and collectively account for 51% of the observed GMSL acceleration. Mountain glaciers contribute an additional 0.01 mm/yr2 to GMSL acceleration, bringing the total land ice contribution to 0.05 ± 0.01 mm/yr2 and thereby partially closing the budget.

title: Seismic Attenuation Tomography of El Hierro: Insights Into Magmatic Processes in the Canary Islands
content:
Abstract
Recent eruptions in the Canary Islands highlight an increase in volcanic activity and provide an exceptional data set to investigate subsurface processes. We present the first 3D seismic attenuation model for the 2011–2012 eruption on El Hierro, using the coda normalization method and a large seismic data set. Our results complement previous 3D velocity models, improving constraints on crustal structure, magma pathways, and intermediate storage zones. The combined interpretation supports a model in which magma ascends from a deep source through structural weaknesses, producing seismic migration patterns linked to eruptive activity. Attenuation anomalies help resolve ambiguities inherent in velocity‐only models, providing a more robust picture of subsurface conditions. These findings offer new insights into magma transport processes and may be extended to interpret recent activity on La Palma and ongoing unrest on Tenerife.

title: Spring Westerly Winds Shape Early Precursors of El Niño Diversity Across the Spring Predictability Barrier
content:
Abstract
Predicting El Niño diversity, specifically the distinction between Eastern Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP) events, remains challenging due to the boreal spring predictability barrier (SPB) and the inconsistent detection inherent in discrete wind‐burst metrics. Here, we present a five‐phase precursor scheme that tracks the monthly evolution of equatorial westerly wind anomalies over 12 months, using wind intensity and spatial centroid metrics from the 1980–2024 reanalysis data. EP and CP precursors diverge as early as boreal spring, when EP‐type wind intensity significantly surpasses CP‐type intensity, whereas CP‐type winds shift anomalously eastward. Spatial composites further reveal an intensity‐position trade‐off governing Kelvin wave excitation, in which stronger wind intensity in EP events compensates for their less favorable, more westward locations. Conversely, meridional centroid tracking fails to discriminate event types until boreal winter. These findings provide a physically interpretable precursor signal for anticipating El Niño within the SPB.

title: Intermediate Water Salinification Counteracts Thermosteric Sea‐Level Rise in the Tropical Southwest Indian Ocean
content:
Abstract
Sea level in the tropical Southwest Indian Ocean has risen rapidly during the Argo era, yet whether its mid‐depth halosteric component reflects along‐isopycnal change or isopycnal displacement remains unresolved. Using gridded Argo data for 2004–2023, we decompose steric sea level into thermosteric and halosteric components and partition temperature and salinity trends into heave (isopycnal displacement) and spice (along‐isopycnal change). Thermosteric expansion is comparable between the upper 300 m and the mid‐depth layer, 300–2,000 m (0.95 ± 0.72 and 1.08 ± 0.17 cm decade−1), though the upper‐layer estimate is less certain. Depth‐integrated halosteric contraction is larger at mid‐depth (−0.20 ± 0.13 and −0.63 ± 0.07 cm decade−1), compensating 58 ± 10% of mid‐depth thermosteric expansion. The mid‐depth salinity trend is overwhelmingly spice‐driven (3:97), so the compensation is primarily along‐isopycnal; the temperature partition (25:75) is weakly constrained. This is consistent with, but does not establish, salinification within the Indian‐sector AAIW‐influenced density range.

title: Tropical Cyclones Increasingly Reach Peak Intensity Near Continental Landfall
content:
Abstract
Tropical cyclones (TCs) typically weaken before landfall after reaching peak intensity over the open ocean. Here we show that this behavior has changed markedly in recent decades. Using global best‐track and reanalysis data sets from 1980 to 2023, we find a significant increase in TCs that intensify within 24 hr of landfall and attain peak intensity at or near the continental coast. Both the frequency and proportion of these events have nearly doubled, with trends concentrated in nearshore regions. This shift is linked to a reorganization of the TC life cycle, characterized by a continentalward migration of TC genesis and increasingly favorable thermodynamic conditions along coastal margins. Climate model simulations indicate that these environmental changes are consistent with anthropogenic warming. The increasing alignment of peak intensity with landfall represents an emerging regime that systematically elevates coastal hazard.
