Soils and their microbiomes are being severely affected by rapid global change. Understanding the effects of anthropogenic stressors on the soil microbiome is therefore key to improving soil resilience and ensuring planetary health. This Focus issue highlights the pressing threats to belowground microbial biodiversity and the opportunities and challenges to restore it.

title: Brain proteinopathies associated physiological changes leading to cognitive resilience in Alzheimer's disease
content: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology has been well characterized, however the molecular mechanisms underlying resilience to the disease remain understudied. With the growing evidence of individuals who are resilient to AD and generation of cross-cohort multiomics data, it has become feasible to understand these mechanisms. In this study, we integrated longitudinal cognitive assessments, regional neuropathology, and matched prefrontal proteomic and metabolomic profiles across donors from two independent cohorts. We identified that asymptomatic AD (AsymAD) brains exhibited amyloid burdens comparable to AD but had fewer compact plaques, lower regional tau burden, and more restricted TDP-43 pathology. Across matched stages of amyloid, tau, and TDP-43 pathology, AsymAD was consistently distinguished from AD by preservation of mitochondrial translation and bioenergetics, synaptic programs, glutamatergic metabolites, and polyunsaturated membrane lipids. Longitudinal cognitive assessments further separated resilient from vulnerable AsymAD individuals despite comparable amyloid and TDP-43 burden, with vulnerability associated with greater neurofibrillary tangle accumulation. Both AsymAD groups retained a prefrontal proteome close to that of cognitively normal individuals, apart from amyloid-associated proteins, whereas mitochondrial, synaptic, and immune changes were largely confined to AD.

title: Generalized inference of noise-corrected state variability in single cells
content: Single-cell omics methods operate at their detection limit and are less conducive to technical controls than mini-bulk approaches, which combine cells of the same type before profiling. To integrate mini-bulk samples with paired split-pool controls more holistically, we built stochprofIC, an algorithm that considers data, noise, and covariates in a distributional-regression framework. We vet stochprofIC with synthetic datasets and compare against an adjusted-variance alternative using mini-bulk data in mouse brains and human breast cancers. The noise-batch corrections provided by stochprofIC enable inference of the single-cell populations comprising the mini-bulk, which are validated repeatedly by RNA FISH in different contexts. We use stochprofIC outputs as input to a systems model of nucleocytoplasmic transport and distinguish heterogeneous trafficking states. Pharmacologic inhibition of a MAP3K11-high state inhibits apoptosis in primary breast-cancer organoids, supporting relevance to phenotypes. By deconvolving changes in location and scale, stochprofIC supports mini-bulking when high-sensitivity and reliability profiles are important.

title: Proton pump inhibitor-associated microbiomes shape systemic host responses
content: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) consistently alter the gut microbiome, but the contribution of these changes to systemic effects associated with PPI use remains unclear. Here, we show that PPI-associated microbiome remodelling induces systemic metabolic and transcriptional responses independently of direct drug exposure. Integrating human microbiome and metabolomics data with metabolic modelling, we identified consistent alterations in microbial metabolic functions and host-microbiome co-metabolism. Transfer of PPI-associated microbiota into germ-free mice reproduced key metabolic changes observed in humans, particularly in aromatic amino acid metabolism, and induced additional alterations in systemic lipid metabolism. These changes were accompanied by tissue-specific transcriptional responses in the colon, liver and brain, affecting metabolic and inflammatory pathways. Together, our findings identify transferable metabolic and transcriptional microbiome-mediated signatures that may contribute to the adverse systemic effects associated with PPI use.

title: scCody distinguishes aging-aligned from divergent disease-associated cellular remodeling
content: Biological aging clocks summarize molecular changes as a single age estimate, but cannot distinguish disease-associated changes that follow healthy aging from those that deviate from it. Here we introduce scCody, a generative framework that learns age-dependent cellular population dynamics from cross-sectional single-cell cohorts using population-level optimal transport and endpoint-consistency regularization. scCody accurately reconstructed cellular populations at unseen ages, recovered age-associated transcriptional changes more effectively than existing generative dynamics models, and enabled donor-age inference without direct age-regression training. Using the learned healthy aging reference, scCody decomposed disease-associated cellular displacement into aging-aligned and orthogonal components. In Alzheimer's disease, selected neuronal populations showed substantial aging-aligned remodeling alongside shared orthogonal changes associated with established pathology signatures. In contrast, COVID-19 exhibited weaker aging alignment and more pronounced orthogonal immune remodeling. Further decomposition revealed patient-level interferon variation associated with symptom duration and increased transcriptional heterogeneity in CD16 monocytes. This framework provides an extension of biological age assessment beyond a single age estimate, distinguishing cellular changes that resemble healthy aging from those that depart from it.

title: Peptide-level assay of protein interaction using combinatorial native and denatured proteolysis
content: Protein protein interactions underlie many extracellular defense and protease regulatory processes, yet identifying their structural interfaces directly in complex biological samples remains challenging. Limited proteolysis coupled with mass spectrometry provides peptide level readouts of local protease accessibility, but linking condition dependent peptide recovery to structural regions in endogenous proteomes requires complementary analysis. Here, we report peptide level assay of protein interaction (PLAPI) using combinatorial native and denatured proteolysis. A single human serum specimen was analyzed in three paired technical preparations using brief trypsin digestion under native conditions and extended digestion after denaturation, followed by isotopic diethyl labeling and LCMS/MS. Applying a 2 of 3 detection rule yielded 920 denatured only peptides and 124 peptides detected under both conditions, with no native only peptides. Mapping to the reference structures placed 13 denatured only C3b peptides at the Factor B binding interface and identified multiple denatured only A2M intersubunit contact regions. Within the A2M bait region, adjacent peptides exhibited different detection patterns; two were detected under both conditions, whereas one was detected only after denaturation. STRING association and enrichment analyses linked the candidate proteins to extracellular defense and protease regulation. These results indicate that PLAPI can provide peptide level evidence for prioritizing structural regions in complex serum samples and guide focused follow up analyses.

title: The absence of microbiome in germ-free mice exacerbates the pathogenicity of mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10
content: Germ-free mice, which are devoid of microbiota, provide a powerful system to define the contribution of the microbiome to host responses during infection. Severe COVID-19 outcomes are associated with multiple comorbidities that are themselves characterized by microbiome dysbiosis; however, the causal role of the microbiota in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we use germ-free mouse models to evaluate the impact of the microbiome on disease severity following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10. Comparison with conventionally housed mice revealed that the absence of the microbiome markedly exacerbates SARS-CoV-2-induced disease in both C57BL/6 and Swiss Webster backgrounds. Germ-free mice exhibited greater weight loss, impaired lung function, worsened pulmonary pathology, and pronounced alterations in circulating cytokine and chemokine profiles compared with conventional controls. These findings show that resident microbiota limit SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity and establish germ-free COVID-19 models as a powerful platform to identify protective microbial taxa and microbiota-based interventions to reduce severe disease.

title: Divergent methane production and microbial community responses to carbon enrichment in freshwater wetland sediments
content: Methane (CH4) accumulation in wetland sediments reflects interactions among organic matter, sediment chemistry, and microbial communities. We combined depth-resolved field characterization across four wetland habitats in northern Israel with complementary incubations to examine methane accumulation and responses to labile-carbon enrichment. Sediment cores were characterized using Rock-Eval analysis, porewater chemistry, oxygen profiling at three sites, and mcrA amplicon sequencing. High CH4 concentrations occurred under contrasting conditions: Ein Nimfit (EN) contained approximately 12% total organic carbon and reached 2.1 mM CH4, whereas Ein Afek site EA2 contained approximately 5% carbon and accumulated 0.7-1.7 mM CH4. Both showed sulfate depletion, but EN exhibited pronounced sulfide accumulation, whereas EA2 showed greater dissolved iron and nutrient enrichment. Their classified methanogenic assemblages also differed. EA1 remained methane poor despite increasing carbon content with depth, while EA3 combined low carbon content and CH4 accumulation with detectable methanogens and lower methanogenic diversity. In a 36-day bottle experiments using sediments from two of the four wetland habitats, sucrose-amended EA3 exhibited a transient maximum of 18.8 mmol collected CH4 kg-1 wet sediment during Days 22-29, whereas EN reached its highest collected amount during Days 29-36. Methane proportions increased before the large output increase in EA3 but remained comparatively stable and high in EN. Soluble chemical oxygen demand trajectories and microbial community changes also differed. These findings identify distinct biogeochemical settings supporting methane accumulation and demonstrate methanogenic potential in low-CH4 sediment, emphasizing the complementary information provided by field profiles, microbial characterization, and exploratory enrichment experiments.

title: Reverse Transcription Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification Combined with Lateral Flow Assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for Rapid Detection of the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus (BDBV) Outbreak Strain
content: Making accurate diagnosis is a critical first step in patient management and control for emerging and re-emerging disease outbreaks. Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is a filovirus that causes Ebola disease, and the 2026 outbreak highlights the need for rapid diagnostic approaches that can be deployed in settings with limited laboratory infrastructure. Here, we developed a reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification-lateral flow assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for rapid detection of the 2026 BDBV outbreak strain. LAMP primers were designed based on the genome sequence of the 2026 outbreak strain, and the conservation of the primer binding sites among all available 2026 outbreak genomes was confirmed in silico. LAMP primers were evaluated for analytical specificity and sensitivity using in vitro-transcribed RNA (ivtRNA) from BDBV and other filoviruses, as well as RNA derived from arboviruses and mammalian cells. Amplification products were detected using a Chromatography-Printed Array Strip (C-PAS) lateral flow platform. The newly designed primers specifically detected the presence of BDBV RNA without nonspecific amplification of the other viral or cellular RNA samples tested. Consistent amplification was observed down to 103 copies per reaction. In addition, BDBV viral RNA was successfully amplified, and the amplification products were detected using C-PAS, with the total workflow being completed within 25 min. These findings demonstrate the analytical specificity and sensitivity of the developed RT-LAMP-LFA assay and its compatibility with rapid visual lateral flow detection, supporting its potential application as a point-of-care approach for BDBV detection.

title: Prevalent Integration of both Xenotropic and Ecotropic Murine Leukemia Virus in the Human Genome of Xenografts
content: Humanized mouse models are widely used in medical research to represent human conditions (1, 2), but their fidelity could be compromised by mouse-originated infections. However, their susceptibility to mouse pathogens are rarely questioned (3). Here we screened 1,619 publicly available genomic sequencing runs from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models for the integration of murine leukemia virus (MLV), a rodent retrovirus exists in the mouse genome as an endogenous retrovirus (4), within the human genome. We discovered substantial enrichment of human-MLV chimeric DNA in approximately 25% of them. Analyzing the human-MLV junctions, we found about 90% of them bearing the unmistakable hallmarks of retroviral integration, including the canonical MLV boundaries and the distinctive 4-bp target site duplications (5, 6). It was also assumed that mouse strains without the highly infectious Bxv1 provirus are safe from MLV contamination in xenografts (7, 8). However, we found many PDX models derived from Bxv1- strains, including the widely used NSG strain, are also contaminated by the supposedly rodent-specific ecotropic MLV (E-MLV). We further confirmed a complete E-MLV integrated into the human genome by both HiFi and sanger sequencing. Our discovery raises concerns that mouse-to-human retroviral transmission and integration is more common and less restrictive than previously appreciated. They support examination of MLV integration as a feature of humanized mouse models with implications on the fidelity of these models in recapitulating human cells and tissues. Our discovery also has underscored the importance of comprehensively inactivation of porcine endogenous retroviruses for the clinical application of xenotransplatation (9, 10).

title: POM121 regulates lentiviral nuclear import in a capsid-host factor-dependent manner
content: Lentiviruses such as human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) access the nuclear lumen through the nuclear pore complex (NPC), a process coordinated by the interactions between the viral capsid and nucleoporins (NUPs). Here, using unbiased proteomic screens, we identified several capsid-associated NUPs, including POM121. Depletion of POM121 impaired HIV-1 infection in multiple cell lines and in primary CD4+ T cells, whereas equine infectious anaemia virus (EIAV) infection was enhanced, indicating that POM121 effect is virus-specific. A cytoplasmic carboxy-terminal fragment of POM121, containing its FG-rich region inhibited HIV-1 and a broader range of lentiviruses. Analysis of HIV-1 capsid mutants showed that physical interaction with POM121 does not predict functional dependence, as capsids retaining POM121 binding remained insensitive to its depletion. Strikingly, loss of cyclophilin A (CypA) completely abolished HIV-1 dependence on POM121, whereas depletion of CPSF6 produced only partial rescue, demonstrating that POM121 sensitivity is dictated by the broader network of capsid-host interactions. Finally, POM121 depletion impaired HIV-1 nuclear accumulation and selectively disrupted the nuclear import of other viral and cellular cargo. Together, these findings identify POM121 as a selective regulator of lentiviral nuclear entry whose functional contribution is determined by capsid and host-factor context.

title: Avian reovirus triggered ferroptosis, modulated lipid metabolism, and induced lipid droplet formation in infected cells, which was mediated in part by the p10/FAST protein
content: In this study, we evaluated how avian reovirus (ARV) affected lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) in cell culture. ARV infection of chicken LMH cells significantly increased the size and number of LDs, however, LDs did not co-localize with virus factories, and neither overexpression by treatment with fatty acids (FAs), nor inhibition by treatment with TOFA or DGAT inhibitors significantly affected ARV replication. Lipidomic analysis revealed that following infection, total cellular lipid content increased approximately 25-fold, phosphatidylcholine (PC) content increased from 23.5 to 57.9%, and the polyunsaturated FA:monounsaturated FA ratio (PUFA:MUFA) decreased in membrane phospholipids but increased in triglycerides. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that there was also a reduction in the expression of genes involved in PUFA synthesis. As membrane PUFAs are susceptible to peroxidation, we investigated whether ARV induced ferroptosis. Consistent with this, ARV led to an increase in oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation that was partially iron dependent, and we found evidence that ferroptosis was proviral. Moreover, as ARV is known to form syncytia, we hypothesized that our observations were also the result of plasma membrane remodeling. Consistent with this, cells transfected with the ARV fusogenic p10/FAST protein formed syncytia, had a significantly upregulated number of LDs, and displayed hallmarks of ferroptosis. Taken together, we hypothesize that ARV induces syncytium formation and ferroptosis to facilitate viral spread to neighboring cells, but to prevent premature cell death due to these processes, lipid metabolism is modulated by infection, leading to an increase in LDs.

title: Hepadnavirus tropism determined by diversified NTCP functionality in Feline species
content: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exhibits a narrow host range, largely determined by sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptides (NTCP), a hepatic bile acid transporter acting as the HBV receptor. NTCP among animals appears to have evolved following trade-off mutations to lose its viral receptor activity while preserving its transporter function. Here, through profiling of the NTCP homologs from 23 mammalian species, we uncover unexpected functional heterogeneity of feline NTCPs. NTCPs derived from cat, tiger, and leopard supported viral preS1 binding and HBV infection, whereas lion-NTCP was deficient for preS1 binding and, notably, exhibited markedly reduced bile acid transport. Cat-NTCP was further demonstrated to have viral receptor function by productive infection in primary cat hepatocytes. Experimental mutagenesis identified double substitution at positions 191 and 268 as key determinants: introducing lion-type substitutions into cat-NTCP (G191R and T268A) abolished preS1 binding, whereas reciprocal substitutions in lion-NTCP restored receptor function. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that lion-NTCP adopts conformation in which a transmembrane helix bending enlarges the whole bile acid tunnel and disrupts preS1 compatibility. Such differences also determined host susceptibility to another feline-infected domestic cat HBV. These findings reveal diversified NTCP functionality with evolutionary plasticity that acquires resistance to hepadnavirus infection at the expense of physiological transporter function.

title: Desiccation stress enhances virulence potential of group B Streptococcus
content: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) asymptomatically inhabits the gastrointestinal and female reproductive tracts but can also cause invasive diseases in susceptible individuals. Despite its clinical importance, relatively little is known about its ability to survive outside the host and whether environmental persistence contributes to transmission and infection. Here we investigate the GBS survival under nutrient starvation and desiccation, characterizing phenotypic and genomic adaptations associated with environmental persistence. GBS remained viable for 30 days during starvation at room temperature and for more than 80 days under desiccated conditions, with GBS grown to stationary-phase bacteria exhibiting greater survival than actively growing bacteria. Survival under desiccation was conserved among several clinically relevant GBS serotypes. Following rehydration desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced biofilm formation compared to control non-desiccated strains. Whole-genome sequencing identified mutations in genes involved in capsule biosynthesis, cell-envelope homeostasis, nutrient transport, and carbohydrate metabolism, suggesting that multiple adaptive pathways may contribute to environmental persistence. Importantly, desiccated GBS retained the capacity to colonize the vaginal mucosa and displayed increased invasion of reproductive tissues in a murine vaginal colonization model. In a systemic infection model, desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced virulence compared to control non-desiccated GBS, demonstrating that environmental survival does not diminish pathogenic potential. This environmental persistence may represent an underappreciated factor contributing to GBS transmission and the epidemiology of late-onset neonatal disease.

title: Elevational variation in gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential across three Himalayan redstart species
content: Environmental gradients and seasonal migration may influence host-associated microbial communities, yet their contributions to gut microbiome variation in montane birds remain poorly understood. We investigated gut microbial communities across 1,300 to 4,200 m in three Himalayan redstarts (Phoenicurus fuliginosus, P. leucocephalus, and P. frontalis) exhibiting contrasting seasonal movement strategies. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 46 fecal samples, we characterized microbial diversity, community composition, distance decay relationships, co-occurrence networks, and predicted functional potential. Elevation was significantly associated with microbial community composition, explaining approximately 3% of variation, whereas host species showed no significant association after accounting for elevation. P. fuliginosus exhibited significant compositional differences among most sampled elevations, whereas P. leucocephalus showed significant positive distance decay relationships. Alpha diversity showed no consistent elevational trend, while core microbial taxa and co-occurrence networks varied among elevational groups. PICRUSt2 analyses identified 28 predicted KEGG Level 3 pathways differing significantly among elevations, including pathways associated with amino acid, lipid, glycan, carbohydrate, and bile acid metabolism. Together, these findings highlight elevation as a significant correlate of gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential, with distinct patterns of microbial turnover among closely related Himalayan redstarts.

title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
content: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.

title: A ribosome-dependent small-ORF switch controls flagellar gene expression and virulence
content: RNA structures are active regulators of bacterial translation. Here, we identified a naturally occurring translation-enhancing small open reading frame (tesORF) that controls the expression of the flagellar operon fliFGHIJK in Salmonella enterica and other motile Enterobacterales. Nucleotide-resolution ribosome profiling revealed this previously unannotated 54-nucleotide ORF immediately upstream of fliF. Genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical analyses support a model in which tesORF translation counteracts an inhibitory RNA structure, exposing the fliF ribosome-binding site and promoting translation initiation independently of the encoded peptide sequence. Disruption of tesORF translation reduced expression of the downstream operon and impaired motility and virulence-associated phenotypes in Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Together, our findings reveal how translation of a conserved small ORF regulates an entire flagellar operon through RNA structural remodelling, with consequences expending to the wider flagellar regulon, linking RNA structural dynamics to bacterial motility and virulence.

title: Necroptosis is a targetable driver of severe coronavirus pathogenesis
content: Human-pathogenic coronaviruses differ dramatically in pathogenicity but the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that highly pathogenic coronaviruses trigger necroptosis in the infected cells and lung tissues, whereas necroptosis is not detected in cells infected by seasonal coronavirus. Mechanistically, highly pathogenic coronaviruses produce Z-RNA, activate ZBP1 and initiates necroptotic cell death signaling, triggering necroinflammation and lung injury. In contrast, seasonal coronaviruses produce little to no Z-RNA, and do not activate necroptosis. Importantly, small-molecule inhibition of necroptosis attenuates inflammatory cytokine expression and markedly ameliorates lung damage in mice infected with all three highly pathogenic coronaviruses, independent of virus clearance. Overall, our study identifies necroptosis as a dominant mediator of coronavirus pathogenesis, and positions necroptosis blockade as a new therapeutic target against severe coronavirus diseases.

title: Herbivore and carnivore microbial signatures indicate diet and health variation in human gut microbiota
content: Diet is a key factor shaping gut microbiota in mammals, with herbivores and carnivores harboring distinct microbial communities. However, despite humans being highly omnivorous, it remains unclear whether their gut microbiota more closely resembles that of herbivores or carnivores or how individual-level variations along this spectrum are associated with human health status. We compared gut microbiota profiles of 858 samples from 109 mammalian species and constructed a Herbivore-Carnivore (HC) index based on bacterial groups characteristic of each diet. The HC-index positioned humans between herbivores and carnivores and showed that traditional hunter-gatherers and nonhuman apes retained herbivore-leaning profiles, whereas urbanized humans exhibited a shift toward a carnivore-leaning state. By applying the HC-index to >72,000 participants across multiple cohorts worldwide, we found that elevated HC-index values were associated with plant-based and fiber-rich diets, greater microbial diversity, enhanced potential to degrade plant-derived carbohydrates, favorable clinical measures, and lower prevalence of self-reported disease. We demonstrated that the HC balance of gut microbiota captures a conserved diet-related gradient across mammals and provides an interpretable framework linking human diet, microbial function, and health.

title: Establishment of split-TurboID in Plasmodium falciparum facilitates identification of a PfAlba2 protein interaction network during late blood stage development
content: Malaria parasites of the genus Plasmodium undergo complex multi-host lifecycles that require precise regulation of gene expression. Unlike model eukaryotes, Plasmodium spp. genomically encodes a limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators, but possess a substantial complement of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms in regulating parasite gene expression. Among these RBPs are a family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins termed 'Alba' (acetylation lowers binding affinity) of which six have so far been identified in these parasites. Here, we investigated the localisation, functional importance and molecular associations of P. falciparum Alba protein PfAlba2 using two different endogenously tagged parasite lines. Using a GFP-FKBP tagged line, we demonstrated that PfAlba2 is expressed throughout asexual blood stage development and primarily localised in the cytosol. Conditional mislocalisation experiments indicated that PfAlba2 contributes to normal parasite growth. To overcome challenges in generating a miniTurboID proximity labelling line, we established a custom split-TurboID proximity labelling system for use in P. falciparum to characterise the PfAlba2 proxiome during asexual blood stage development. The split-TurboID system facilitated identification of 101 enriched PfAlba2 proximal proteins in schizont stage development, with significant enrichment for proteins involved in translation initiation, including two additional Alba family members, PfAlba1 and PfAlba4. Complementary RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 380 PfAlba2-associated transcripts with significant enrichments including cytosolic ribosomes, rRNA-processing factors, PfAlba1, and egress and invasion-related transcripts (PfRALP1, PfRON4, PfRH1, PfRH5). Together, these findings implicate PfAlba2 in RNA metabolism and translational regulation, suggesting an important regulatory function for this protein during parasite blood stage development.

title: A Xenopus laevis Model for Systemic Fungal Infections
content: Xenopus laevis possesses both innate and adaptive immune systems, and we previously demonstrated its utility as an infection model for human bacterial pathogens. In this study, we investigated the utility of X. laevis as a model for fungal infections. The human-pathogenic fungi Candida albicans and Aspergillus fumigatus exhibited greater lethality in X. laevis than the nonpathogenic fungi Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe. In frogs infected with C. albicans, viable fungal cells were detected in the blood and multiple organs early after infection, and gross white lesions and fungal hyphae were observed in the kidneys. C. albicans infection also increased renal expression of the proinflammatory cytokine gene s tnf and il1b, as well as the tissue injury-associated gene clu. Treatment with the antifungal agents amphotericin B and micafungin significantly improved the survival of C. albicans-infected frogs. Furthermore, a homozygous deletion mutant of UME6, a gene associated with C. albicans virulence, exhibited reduced lethality compared with the wild-type strain. These findings establish X. laevis as a vertebrate model of systemic fungal infection that enables the evaluation of fungal virulence, host responses, and the therapeutic efficacy of antifungal agents.

title: Functional characterisation and identification of a core interactome of Plasmodium regulatory protein Alba4
content: Plasmodium spp. parasites have complex lifecycles that rely on strict regulation of gene and protein expression. Current evidence suggests that P. falciparum has a relatively limited repertoire of canonical transcriptional regulators and RNA interference (RNAi)-associated small RNAs compared to model eukaryotes, potentially reflecting a greater reliance on RNA binding protein (RBP)-mediated post-transcriptional regulation (PTR). Among these RBPs, the acetylation lowers binding affinity (Alba) family of DNA/RNA-binding proteins has been implicated in RNA metabolism and regulation of mRNA stability and translation. In Plasmodium spp. parasites, the Alba family has expanded to include up to six members, with sequence divergence and structural modifications beyond the conserved Alba domain leading to diversification of family members, some of which appear restricted to Plasmodium and related parasites. In this study, we were unable to truncate PfAlba4, but successfully generated an endogenously tagged PfAlba4 parasite line, representing the first successful instance of endogenous tagging of a PfAlba family protein. Utilising this transgenic line, we confirm ubiquitous expression throughout blood stage development and its predominantly cytosolic localisation. Conditional loss of PfAlba4 through the knock-sideways approach demonstrated an important role for PfAlba4 in blood stage development and proteomics analysis defined a protein interaction network of 67 significantly enriched proteins, with notable enrichment of proteins potentially involved in RNA processing and regulation. Further characterisation of one of these proteins, the uncharacterised protein PF3D7_0706500, revealed a partially overlapping network of proximal proteins enriched for RNA-regulatory factors, suggesting potentially shared roles in PTR. RNA Immunoprecipitation-Sequencing (RIP-seq) identified 692 PfAlba4 associated transcripts, with an enrichment of a pyrimidine-rich motif in their 3' untranslated regions, suggesting a potential sequence-dependent mechanism of RNA recognition. Integration of proteomic and RIP-Seq datasets in late blood stage parasites revealed a consistent association with RNA processing and regulatory pathways, implicating PfAlba4 in post-transcriptional regulation. Together these findings establish PfAlba4 as an important component of the RNA-regulatory landscape in P. falciparum and highlight the importance of PfAlba proteins for malaria parasite blood stage development.

title: NON-NUCLEOSIDE REVERSE TRANSCRIPTASE INHIBITORS BLOCK THE INCORPORATION OF VIRAL GLYCOPROTEINS INTO HIV-1 VIRIONS
content: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) are a key component of antiretroviral therapy that block reverse transcription in newly infected cells. NNRTIs have also been reported to induce premature activation of the HIV-1 protease in virus-producing cells, an activity that has been optimized in a class of NNRTIs known as targeted activators of cell kill (TACK). In this study, we used the TACK compound Pyr01 to investigate how NNRTI-induced premature protease activation affects virion composition and infectivity. We found that Pyr01 treatment markedly reduces the incorporation of the HIV-1 envelope (Env) glycoprotein into virus particles in an Env cytoplasmic tail-independent manner. Pyr01 treatment also disrupts the virion incorporation of foreign viral glycoproteins and causes a substantial loss of the viral enzymes from virions. Virions produced from NNRTI-treated cells exhibit reduced membrane order. The defect in viral glycoprotein incorporation requires an active protease, implicating premature protease-mediated disruption of the Gag lattice and resulting changes in membrane properties as the primary mechanism underlying these effects. These findings reveal that NNRTI-induced premature protease activation during virus assembly fundamentally changes the protein composition and membrane order of HIV-1 virions to markedly reduce particle infectivity. These results have implications for the use of TACK compounds therapeutically and provide basic insights into the properties of the viral membrane that promote viral glycoprotein incorporation.

title: Heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 Attenuates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Intestinal Inflammation and Barrier Disruption
content: Intestinal barrier dysfunction and excessive inflammation contribute to the pathogenesis of various metabolic and gastrointestinal diseases. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induces systemic and intestinal inflammation, disrupts epithelial tight junctions, and impairs intestinal barrier integrity. Although heat-killed Latilactobacillus sakei D279 exhibits antiviral activity, its effects on intestinal barrier function remain unclear. In this study, we examined whether heat-killed D279 preserves intestinal barrier integrity and attenuates LPS-induced inflammatory responses in vivo (LPS-challenged mice), ex vivo (mouse peritoneal macrophages), and in vitro (IEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells). Cytokine and receptor gene expression in macrophages was measured to evaluate inflammatory responses. Furthermore, barrier function was assessed using transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), and the expression of tight junction-related genes was assessed. D279 alleviated LPS-induced intestinal injury in LPS-challenged mice, as indicated by the attenuation of colon shortening and histopathological changes compared to those in the LPS control group. In peritoneal macrophages, D279 pretreatment suppressed LPS-induced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-, IL-1{beta}, and IL-12{beta}), increased IL-10 expression, and reduced LPS-induced upregulation of MLCK expression. This postbiotic increased basal cell viability in a concentration-dependent manner in IEC-6 cells. Moreover, it enhanced epithelial barrier development (increased TEER) and upregulated tight junction gene expression. These findings demonstrate that heat-killed D279 primarily confers its benefits by attenuating LPS-induced cytokine responses, limiting the upregulation of MLCK expression, and partially preserving goblet cell abundance. This is consistent with its protective postbiotic role in intestinal homeostasis. Thus, this study introduces a candidate postbiotic for the promotion of intestinal resilience under systemic inflammatory stress.

title: Sphingolipid Hydroxylation Governs Fungal Pathogenicity and Drug Susceptibility: Scs7 as a Druggable Target in Candida albicans
content: Sphingolipids are essential structural components of the fungal plasma membrane and key signaling hubs that orchestrate pathogenicity. While both fungi and mammals perform sphingolipid hydroxylation, they rely on evolutionarily divergent enzymatic systems, establishing a biochemical divergence exploitable for selective targeting. Here, through a screening of sphingolipid metabolic genes, we identify the sphingolipid -hydroxylase Scs7 as a central regulator of membrane homeostasis, virulence, and caspofungin susceptibility in Candida albicans. Genetic ablation of SCS7 depletes hydroxylated sphingolipids, disrupts memberane organization, and compromises cell wall integrity, which collectively impair hyphal morphogenesis, biofilm formation, and stress tolerance through blockade of the cAMP-PKA signaling axis. In a murine cutaneous infection model, SCS7 deletion markedly attenuates fungal burden, hyperinflammation, and epidermal barrier disruption, underscoring its non-redundant role in host-pathogen interaction. Leveraging the fungus-specific architecture of Scs7, we performed virtual screening and identified resveratrol as a natural Scs7 inhibitor. Resveratrol recapitulates the lipidomic and phenotypic defects of SCS7 deletion and synergizes with caspofungin to enhance fungal killing. Our study establishes sphingolipid -hydroxylation as a master determinant of fungal membrane fitness and validates Scs7 as a promising, fungus-specific antifungal target with dual anti-virulence and chemosensitizing activities.

title: Evolutionarily distinct dengue virus type 2 with a unique type-specific neutralization determinant
content: Dengue viruses 1-4 (DENV1-4) mostly circulate in endemic cycles involving humans and Aedes mosquitoes. However, rare dengue outbreaks originate from non-human primates. These spillovers are caused by sylvatic virus genotypes that are closely related to endemic strains of the same serotype, but some are caused by strains that fall between the four canonical serotypes on phylogenetic trees. It is not clear whether these genotypic differences are reflected in corresponding antigenic differences. Here, we characterized the antigenic features of QML-22, a divergent strain most closely related to DENV2. On an antigenic map, QML-22 clustered with other globally representative DENV2 strains. QML-22 was not as well neutralized by antisera raised against endemic DENV2 and was better neutralized by antisera from DENV1, 3, and 4 infections than other strains of DENV2. QML-22 had a cluster of distinct amino acid residues in domain I of the envelope (E) protein, with only scattered point mutations elsewhere in the envelope. A potently neutralizing anti-DENV2 antibody that targets this site in domain I of the E protein, 3F9, had >1000-fold lower neutralization of QML-22 than other endemic DENV2 strains, whereas other cross-reactive and DENV2-specific antibodies neutralized QML-22 and endemic strains to similar titers. When antisera from non-human primates infected with QML-22 or DENV2 reference strain S16803 were depleted with the heterologous virions, homologous neutralization was unaffected but heterologous neutralization was reduced, suggesting homologous neutralization was due to distinct epitopes. Evolutionary analyses showed the 3F9 epitope was under relaxed selection pressure compared to other neutralizing epitopes and that QML-22 had unique amino acids in this epitope relative to the likely common ancestor of all DENV2. These findings provide insight into the antigenic diversification of DENV and the possible evolution of new serotypes.

title: A vulnerability assessment framework for terrestrial invertebrate species threatened by wildlife trade
content: Wildlife trade is an emerging threat to terrestrial invertebrates in Australia, yet its impact on native populations remains poorly quantified. Short range endemic (SRE) species, often characterised by restricted geographic ranges, low reproductive output, low vagility, and specialised habitat conditions, are particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, including over-exploitation via wild harvesting. Using a multi-year dataset of Australian invertebrate trade records, we identified species that are both utilised in the pet trade and exhibiting SRE traits, and assessed their risk of population decline by integrating trade frequency with species distribution, abundance, and biological vulnerability. We identified 266 species traded in Australia with an area of occupancy less than 500 square kilometres, with arachnids disproportionately represented among those at greatest relative risk of population decline from over-exploitation. While these rankings should be interpreted as a methodological demonstration rather than a definitive measure of extinction risk, they provide a transparent approach for screening species where trade pressure may intersect with biological vulnerability. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first tested approach to holistically assess this risk in invertebrates. We present a proof-of-concept framework for quantifying trade-related vulnerability in terrestrial invertebrates, providing a transferable approach that can be refined and applied across a wide range of taxa threatened by wildlife trade.

title: Dog-assisted scat sampling reveals genetic diversity, structure, and relatedness in black-footed cats (Felis nigripes)
content: Advances in molecular techniques for non-invasive genetic sampling have strengthened wildlife genetics, enabling researchers to study elusive and difficult-to-study species with minimal disturbance, and conservation detection dogs can greatly increase sample numbers and the area covered. However, this combination is rarely used in Africa and has perhaps never been applied to a small carnivore on the continent. Here we use dog-assisted scat surveys to carry out the first fine-scale population genetic study of the black-footed cat (Felis nigripes), Africa's smallest and most range-restricted endemic felid, and a threatened species for which conventional survey methods are largely ineffective. Using 130 successfully genotyped scat samples (nine microsatellite loci) from two populations about 650 km apart, we identified 65 individuals and assessed genetic diversity and fine-scale relatedness to explore aspects of dispersal and reproductive ecology. Both populations exhibited similar observed heterozygosity (Ho = 0.67-0.69) and allelic richness, with no heterozygote deficit (FIS = -0.02 to -0.08). Differentiation between the southern Namibia and central South Africa sites was low but detectable (FST = 0.03-0.05). We used pairwise relatedness and candidate pedigree results to explore hypotheses about sex-specific relatedness patterns. Female-female dyads were more related than male-male dyads at the shortest distance class (0-2 km), a pattern compatible with female philopatry. There were more half-sibling than full-sibling assignments and uneven representation of candidate fathers, which may indicate polygamy and reproductive skew. These results provide baseline genetic data for a Vulnerable species and show that this approach is feasible for Africa's small, elusive carnivores, whose dispersal, mating systems and population structure remain largely unknown. Broader spatial and temporal sampling could help assess population connectivity and reveal how threats and changing land use impact genetic diversity and structure.

title: Is hidden demographic heterogeneity pervasive? Harvested birds as an example
content: Individual demographic heterogeneity refers to the fact that individuals from a given population exposed to similar environmental conditions express different demographic traits or tactics. This heterogeneity can either be linked to factors/states such as age, sex or body condition, or be due to hidden factors/states not immediately apparent or easily characterized (hereinafter referred to as 'hidden heterogeneity'). Yet accounting for demographic heterogeneity, and more particularly heterogeneity in survival is crucial because it is an important mechanism underlying compensation processes between natural and harvest mortality. In this study, we used capture-mark-recapture-recovery data of 6 hunted species covering a large range of the demographic slow-fast continuum (61,432 individuals ringed from 1953 to 2020 among Common Teal Anas crecca, Mallard A. platyrhynchos, Common Pochard Aythya ferina, Common Snipe Gallinago gallinago, Common quail Coturnix coturnix, and Blackbird Turdus merula), to assess the presence of unexplained heterogeneity in survival with multievent models. We detected hidden survival heterogeneity in most species, even though the differences between the high and low categories of survival were often small. The probability for an individual to display a low vs high survival rate was not related to potentially important individual factors/states such as migration phenology or to morphology. The presence of hidden heterogeneity was pervasive, affecting species distributed along a relatively large spectrum of demographic strategies. This, in our opinion, supports that part of this heterogeneity in survival evidenced in our study is indeed hidden, resulting either from hidden intrinsic (inherent) individual differences of survival among individuals, or hidden extrinsic factors e.g., linked to spatial variations in hunting pressure. Our findings suggest that hidden heterogeneity needs to be explored more thoroughly in huntable species and accounted for in management policies.

title: Depth structures metabolic potential and warming responses inmarine microbial eukaryotes
content: Microbial eukaryotes are key drivers of food-web dynamics and nutrient cycling across the ocean's water column. Yet, how their metabolic potential is structured through depth remains largely unknown, limiting our ability to understand how microbial communities mediate biogeochemical transformations and how these functions may shift under climate change. Here, we combined a global-scale metagenomic analysis of tropical and subtropical samples spanning the full water column with bathypelagic metatranscriptomics to identify depth-dependent functional patterns across plankton size fractions. At depth, the functional composition of the nanoplankton size fraction was consistent with the export of surface-derived biomass, whereas the picoplankton size fraction showed signatures of resident communities, including depth-specific heterotrophic functions and bathypelagic-restricted fungal assemblages. Metabolic functional diversity was tightly coupled to taxonomic composition along the water column. Heterotrophic lineages contributed to phosphorus and sulfur acquisition at depth, revealing an undercharacterised eukaryotic role in deep-ocean nutrient cycling. Projections under end-of-century warming revealed spatially structured metabolic responses: subtropical intensification of photosynthetic capacity, subpolar stimulation of aerobic metabolism, and a decline of heterotrophic potential consistent with metabolic rebalancing within mixotrophic taxa. Our findings highlight the importance of marine microbial eukaryotes in ocean biogeochemistry, reveal their distinct functional roles across depths, and provide novel projections of how their metabolic potential may change under ocean warming.

title: Effects of tree species diversity and identity on remotely sensed canopy variables in two forest biodiversity experiments
content: Remote sensing can link biodiversity and its effects on ecosystem functioning in forests, but in observational studies environmental covariates may confound results. We tested effects of tree species richness and functional diversity on remotely-sensed canopy variables at community and species levels in two forest biodiversity experiments established under homogeneous environmental conditions. At the BIOTREE sites in Kaltenborn and Bechstedt, we combined airborne imaging spectroscopy-based vegetation indices, sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence, and land surface temperature at 1-m resolution, with ground-based tree stem growth as a productivity measure. At Kaltenborn, increasing species richness (one to four species) did not increase community productivity because of contrasting species-level responses. The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) decreased with richness in both needle-leaved species but increased in both broadleaved species. At Bechstedt, increasing functional diversity of mixtures planted with four tree species lowered community-level normalized difference water and photochemical reflectance indices; responses differed between four functional groups of tree species. NDVI was negatively correlated with basal area; correlations among other spectral, thermal, and fluorescence traits varied among tree functional groups. These results show that forest biodiversity experiments can test remotely sensed indicators of tree diversity and ecosystem functioning and inform interpretation of observational studies.

title: A leaf-carbon economy model to explain the adaptive value of low vs. high leaf mass per area as a function of habitat productivity
content: Plant traits interact with environmental conditions to determine plant fitness. In particular, plant species with low leaf mass per area (LMA) are more common in high fertility soils and forest gaps, while plant species with high LMA are more common in low fertility soils and in shaded forest understories. It is not yet known why the adaptive value of LMA changes as a function of environmental productivity. We present a model for plant growth as a function of LMA and productivity. Our model relies on an empirically derived relationship between LMA and leaf lifespan. We are able to explain why species with lower LMA are successful in high productivity environments including environments with high availability of either light or soil nutrients, by showing that the LMA which maximizes growth rate decreases with increasing rate of carbon assimilation. We show that low LMA species are better at taking advantage of the 'high interest' environment of high productivity habitats by reinvesting assimilated carbon in new leaves and earning compound interest, while high LMA species grow more efficiently in the 'low interest' environment of low productivity habitats. This tradeoff sheds light on the adaptive value of LMA as it relates to environmental productivity.

title: Fungal-bacterial interactions enhance bacterial but constrain fungal resistance and recovery to extreme heat across soil moisture levels
content: Soil fungi and bacteria are key drivers of nutrient cycling and plant productivity in terrestrial ecosystems, yet their responses to climate extremes are rarely studied as interacting partners rather than in isolation. Moreover, it remains largely unknown how fungal-bacterial interactions regulate fungal and bacterial stability under climate extremes, particularly resistance (immediate responses to climate extremes) and recovery (responses after climate extremes cease). Here, we conducted a soil microcosm experiment with a bacterial species (Pseudomonas putida KT2440) paired with one of four Trichoderma species (T. hamatum, T. atroviride, T. koningiopsis, and T. harzianum). These fungal-bacterial pairs were then exposed to a 5-day heat event (40 {degrees}C/32 {degrees}C, day/night) followed by a 14-day recovery period (25 {degrees}C/17 {degrees}C, day/night), at two soil moisture levels (30% and 5% gravimetric water content). Our results show that fungal-bacterial interactions asymmetrically affect fungal and bacterial responses to extreme heat. Trichoderma species facilitated the resistance and recovery of P. putida density (CFUs) to extreme heat, whereas P. putida constrained the resistance and recovery of fungal biomass (ergosterol) to extreme heat, regardless of soil moisture conditions. Moreover, faster-growing Trichoderma species were associated with greater facilitation of bacterial resistance and recovery. Bacterial density also covaried positively with fungal biomass during heat stress under both soil moisture conditions, suggesting that net fungal facilitation enhances bacterial persistence under extreme heat. Together, our findings reveal that fungal-bacterial interactions can stabilize one microbial partner while increasing the vulnerability of the other, highlighting the contrasting consequences of biotic interactions under climate extremes.

title: Species differentiate water uptake depths within a narrow vertical zone in temperate grasslands
content: Whether and under which conditions coexisting species in temperate grasslands differentiate their water uptake within the shallow soil layer they share is central to understanding hydrological niche differentiation in these ecosystems. In this field study, we quantified water uptake depth of 28 coexisting herbaceous species across 74 temperate grassland plots in three regions of Germany using oxygen stable isotopes and soil water content measured at multiple depths. Species consistently differed in water uptake depth across all regions, consistent with hydrological niche differentiation. This differentiation was largely confined to the upper 30 cm of soil and became stronger as overall soil moisture declined, with plants accessing water at greater depths in drier plots. In contrast, the vertical distribution of soil moisture was unrelated to either uptake depth or species differentiation. Despite pronounced species level variation, broad herbaceous functional classifications, including grasses versus forbs and fibrous versus taprooted species, showed substantial overlap in water uptake depth. Together, our results show that hydrological niche differentiation in temperate grasslands is expressed through fine scale differences among species within a shared shallow soil domain, becomes more pronounced under drier conditions, and is poorly captured by broad herbaceous functional classifications.
